title: The Access Layer of AI Visibility: A robots.txt Census and Policy-Diffusion Analysis of AI-Crawler Blocking Across 100 Indonesian News Media (2020-2026)
affiliations: Universitas Prasetiya Mulya

detail.title: The Access Layer of AI Visibility: A robots.txt Census and Policy-Diffusion Analysis of AI-Crawler Blocking Across 100 Indonesian News Media (2020-2026)
detail.abstract: Generative search engines answer questions by synthesizing a small set of retrieved web sources, making whether and how an organization's content can be surfaced a strategic problem — the concern this paper frames as AI Visibility Optimization (AIVO). AIVO has so far been examined mostly at the contentselection layer, where Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) shows that page-level tactics can raise the odds of being cited (Aggarwal et al., 2024). Logically prior to selection, however, is a supply-side question rarely measured in emerging markets: can AI crawlers reach the content at all? This paper isolates that access layer. Motivated by prior audits in which Indonesian mainstream media appear only sparingly among the sources generative systems cite (Budiman, 2026b, 2026c), I test one intuitive supply-side explanation — that publishers withhold content from AI crawlers through the Robots Exclusion Protocol (robots.txt) — and largely reject it. Using an honest, rate-limited crawler I collected the current robots.txt of 100 Indonesian news outlets across national, business/specialist, regional, and digital-native tiers, coding directives for 16 named AI crawlers (training and retrieval) plus two conventional search bots as controls, and reconstructed each outlet's policy history from the Internet Archive Wayback Machine (2020–2026, monthly resolution). Blocking is uncommon. GPTBot, the most-blocked crawler, is fully disallowed by just 20% of readable outlets (95% Wilson CI 13–29%) — far below the 48–79% reported for high-income markets (Fletcher, 2024) — and 77% declare no AI-crawler policy at all. Even these rates are an upper bound on the national picture: only 5.8% of Indonesian news sites generally block AI crawlers and only 40.3% carry a robots.txt file at all (Dhyatmika et al., 2026), against 97 of the 100 outlets sampled here. Most consequentially for AIVO, 85% of outlets are fully open to every retrieval crawler — the agents that ground live cited answers — and no outlet blocks retrieval without also blocking training. Control crawlers are never fully blocked, validating the coding. The salient gap is organizational rather than geographic: digital-native outlets are almost entirely open (95% zero-policy), and policy is not uniform within media groups. Longitudinally, the first AI-crawler directives appear in May 2023; the largest single-month wave of adoption falls in October 2023, two months after GPTBot's release, after which cumulative adoption plateaus near 44% of archived outlets — an Indonesian echo of the global “rapid crescendo” (Longpre et al., 2024), readable through a diffusion-of-innovations lens (Rogers, 2003). Read together with evidence that blocking rarely prevents citation anyway (Longpre et al., 2024), the results imply that the scarcity of Indonesian mainstream media in generative answers is a demand-side (modelselection) phenomenon, not publisher opt-out. The paper contributes the first cross-domain, longitudinal robots.txt census for Indonesia — complementing qualitative and traffic-based Indonesian work (Dhyatmika et al., 2026) with a per-crawler, per-outlet record of declarations; positions it as the access layer of an AI Visibility Supply Chain linking crawlability, provenance interpretability, and citation selection; and, consistent with the field's limitations, frames robots.txt as declared intent rather than enforced access.

title: Signal, Gate, Consider, Decide: A Process Framework for AI-Mediated B2B Vendor Discovery

detail.title: Signal, Gate, Consider, Decide: A Process Framework for AI-Mediated B2B Vendor Discovery
detail.abstract: AI answer engines increasingly mediate how business buyers discover vendors, citing a small set of names from a much larger competitive field. Four established literatures, gatekeeping theory, consideration-set theory, organizational buying theory, and signaling theory, each explain a piece of this process, but no published framework connects them, despite each describing an adjacent link in what this paper argues is a single causal sequence. This paper integrates the four into a four-stage process framework: vendor signal strength shapes algorithmic citation selection, citation selection shapes the buyer's evoked consideration set, and the buyer's reliance on that set shifts by purchase stage and buying-center role. A fifth link closes the sequence into a selfreinforcing loop, in which citation success funds further signal investment, consistent with cumulative-advantage dynamics documented since Merton's (1968) Matthew effect. The framework extends signaling theory, rather than introducing a separate construct, to treat vendor incumbency as a status-based signal following Podolny's (1993) model of market competition, and it scopes its central mechanism explicitly to retrieval-grounded AI architectures, distinguishing this account from source-fabrication dynamics documented in ungrounded language models. Five falsifiable propositions follow from the integration, along with stated boundary conditions and a research agenda naming the specific empirical studies, including a matched-pairs test of the incumbency moderation and an intervention design testing the compounding claim, that the framework implies but does not itself execute. The contribution is an integrative, generative synthesis: four adjacent literatures organized into one testable process.

title:
From Job Description to Purpose

Description: An Organizational Theory of Dynamic Role Design and Future Value Creation in the Age of AI

detail.title:
From Job Description to Purpose

Description: An Organizational Theory of Dynamic Role Design and Future Value Creation in the Age of AI
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly expanding the scope of analysis, prediction,
generation, decision support, and task execution, rendering human roles within firms
increasingly fluid. In many organizations, however, roles are still defined around the
Job Description (JD)—a collection of assigned tasks, areas of responsibility, required
competencies, and reporting relationships. While this static allocation model serves
stable divisions of labor well, it cannot adequately express the purpose of a role or the
value it creates in environments where the mapping between tasks and humans
changes continuously and the human-AI collaborative system itself becomes an object
of redesign.
Connecting work design theory with dynamic capabilities research, this paper
proposes the Purpose Description (PD), a concept of dynamic role design positioned
above the JD. A PD is an organizational design unit that articulates—in light of the
future expectations shared by markets and society and the future the firm seeks to
realize—why an individual or team exists, for whom it creates what future value, and on
the basis of which questions and decision principles it acts.
The paper’s central thesis is that whereas a JD allocates present tasks, a PD distributes
the creation of future value. The PD is positioned as structural middleware that connects the market’s expectations of the future captured by Future Value Theory
(Kadowaki, 2026a) and the continuous redesign of the enterprise addressed by
Enterprise Redefinition (Kadowaki, 2026b) to the actions of individuals and teams.
The paper presents a Two-Tier Dynamic Role Architecture that integrates PD and JD as
complements, together with a synchronization protocol. It further sets out the causal
mechanism by which purposeless local optimization in AI adoption is avoided, nine
testable propositions, directions for measurement, legal and labor governance,
safeguards against over-adaptation, and human authority to halt AI systems. The
creation of future value depicted by the PD and the execution of PD-defined roles are
carried out by integrated human-AI systems, but the determination of purpose and
decision principles, exception handling, halt authority, and legal and ethical
accountability remain vested in humans. The PD does not substitute for working
conditions, authority, or accountability; it preserves them while placing existential
purpose and the connection to future value above ever-changing means.

title: Impacts of Noisy Certification and Price Signaling on Product Quality Disclosure
affiliations: National Taiwan University, Hong Kong Polytechnic University - Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies and Hong Kong Polytechnic University - Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies

detail.title: Impacts of Noisy Certification and Price Signaling on Product Quality Disclosure
detail.abstract: This study investigates the strategic interaction between noisy certification and price signaling of product quality. We develop a game-theoretic model in which costly and imperfect certification is available to a firm, under both mandatory and voluntary regimes. Our analysis explores the firm's decisions regarding certification application and pricing, the impact of certification accuracy and associated costs, and the design of certification schemes. We find that noisy certification reshapes the role of price signaling and that the voluntary certification decision is jointly determined by accuracy and costs. When certification is sufficiently accurate and moderately costly, the high-quality firm applies, whereas the low-quality firm is deterred. In particular, the high-quality firm can mitigate or eliminate price distortion upon successful certification, while failure restores subsequent pricing as a signaling device. Relative to the no-certification benchmark, we show that voluntary certification generally benefits firms, whereas mandatory certification may harm high-quality firms but benefit low-quality firms under low accuracy and moderate costs. Comparing regimes, high-quality firms prefer voluntary certification, whereas low-quality firms favor mandatory certification when accuracy is insufficient. Our findings provide managerial insights for policymakers, emphasizing the need to assess certification accuracy and costs in deciding between mandatory and voluntary regimes.

title: Converting Browsers to Buyers: Exploring What Drives Consumer Choice in Internet E-Commerce

detail.title: Converting Browsers to Buyers: Exploring What Drives Consumer Choice in Internet E-Commerce
detail.abstract: Why do internet users behave as they do, are their activities solely determined by website design? Or do they create their own pathways as a response to designated systems. For many, internet design is about the imposition of schemas, predetermined flows and consumer motifs, allowing the shepherding of an understood and mapped user towards buying products and services. However, if this were true then every browser would also be a buyer. The underlying concepts of current website design rely on a number of pretexts which, when reviewed in relation to human activity and interaction, become questionable in their veracity.

title: Learning While Earning: Algorithmic Learning and Pricing Strategies in Ship-Then-Shop Retailing
affiliations: Tsinghua University - Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University - Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management and Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business

detail.title: Learning While Earning: Algorithmic Learning and Pricing Strategies in Ship-Then-Shop Retailing
detail.abstract: In algorithm-driven ship-then-shop (STS) retailing, retailers ship preselected products to customers for trial before purchase. Yet STS retailers exhibit striking pricing heterogeneity, relying on subscription fees, product prices, or both. We develop a two-period game-theoretic model to explain this divergence, endogenizing how consumer subscriptions and subsequent keep-or-return decisions generate the data required to improve matching accuracy. We model three key algorithmic characteristics: the cold-start threshold, learning capacity, and baseline matching probability. Driven by the tension between data acquisition and data monetization, we first identify three optimal pricing regimes-ex-ante, balanced, and ex-post extraction. When the coldstart threshold is low, the retailer adopts ex-ante extraction (subscription fee only) or balanced extraction (both a subscription fee and a product price), depending on learning capacity; when the threshold is high, it adopts ex-post extraction (product price only). Second, a higher cold-start threshold lowers the subscription fee to attract the larger subscriber base needed for data acquisition, whereas the product price can respond non-monotonically as the retailer balances higher margins from successful matches against the loss of future subscription demand. Third, greater learning capacity makes successful future matches more likely, shifting revenue extraction toward the product price. Fourth, a higher baseline matching probability induces a quasiconcave response in the subscription fee and a quasiconvex response in the product price. Finally, a higher proportion of churn-prone consumers limits future monetization, shifting revenue extraction toward the subscription fee to capture more revenue before consumers churn.

title: The Safety Illusion: How the Mere Presence of a Dislike Button Shapes Belief in Social Media Content
affiliations: , Ivy College of Business, University of Florida and Harvard Business School

detail.title: The Safety Illusion: How the Mere Presence of a Dislike Button Shapes Belief in Social Media Content
detail.abstract: Prior research shows that visible engagement metrics, such as counts of likes, dislikes, and shares, can influence perceived content credibility. The present research examines whether the mere presence of a negative engagement affordance-a dislike button-can shape credibility judgments even when it provides no publicly visible information about how other users evaluated the content. Classic belief-formation theories suggest that such a negative affordance should prompt skepticism and lower perceived credibility. However, across one large-scale analysis of real-world social media comments (N = 40,458) and four controlled experiments (N = 1,845), the findings show that the presence of a dislike button increases perceived credibility. This effect occurs because consumers interpret the button as a signal that the platform can monitor, filter, or regulate low-quality content, creating an illusion of platform-level protection from misinformation. Consistent with this mechanism, the effect is attenuated when consumers are explicitly informed that the platform takes steps to reduce misinformation. This research advances understanding of consumer belief formation in digital environments by showing that engagement affordances can serve not only as tools for user interaction, but also as platformlevel signals that shape how consumers judge content credibility.

detail.abstract:
Customer satisfaction is an important indicator of service performance in the banking sector, particularly for rural banking institutions that play a significant role in promoting financial inclusion and rural development. The present study examines customer satisfaction towards the services of Meghalaya Rural Bank in East Khasi Hills District, Meghalaya. Specifically, the study seeks to examine the factors associated with customer satisfaction and assess customers' perceptions regarding the banking facilities provided by the bank. The study adopted a descriptive research design and was based on primary data collected from 114 customers of Meghalaya Rural Bank through a structured questionnaire. A convenience sampling technique was employed, and the collected data were analysed using frequency distributions and percentage analysis.

The findings indicate that customers generally hold favourable perceptions towards the services provided by Meghalaya Rural Bank. Positive evaluations were particularly observed regarding the bank’s role in promoting rural development, customer trust, simplicity of banking procedures, and satisfaction with banking facilities. The findings further suggest that convenience and trust are important considerations in customers’ association with the bank. However, comparatively lower positive responses were observed with respect to service efficiency, information regarding new services, and the reasonableness of interest rates and charges, indicating scope for improvement in these areas.

The study highlights the importance of maintaining customer-oriented services, strengthening communication initiatives, and enhancing service efficiency to improve customer satisfaction and reinforce the role of Meghalaya Rural Bank in promoting financial inclusion and rural development.

title: Impact of Digital Marketing on Sales Growth of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in the e-commerce Sector of Bangladesh
affiliations: East West University

detail.title: Impact of Digital Marketing on Sales Growth of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in the e-commerce Sector of Bangladesh

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved an anonymous online survey of business owners. Participation was voluntary, and no personally identifiable information was collected. Formal institutional ethics board approval was not sought, as is standard for undergraduate coursework research of this nature.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates how major digital marketing tools-specifically Search Engine Optimization (SEO), keyword optimization, behavioral targeting, and online advertising-influence the sales growth of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) operating within B2B and B2C e-commerce models in Bangladesh. A quantitative research design is adopted, utilizing primary data gathered through a survey of 250 SME owners and entrepreneurs. Contextualizing the study with existing literature, benchmark data indicate that keyword optimization can improve sales conversion rates by approximately 24-40% (Gupta and Bansal, 2023), and behavioral targeting can increase click-through rates by up to 670% (Yan et al., 2009). Furthermore, AI-driven marketing practices have been shown to reduce advertising expenses by 23.5% and enhance returns by 52.9% (Sun and Yu, 2025). Although these advantages are documented in great detail, the primary survey findings reveal a critically low rate of adoption among Bangladeshi SMEs. Currently, only 19.6% actively use digital marketing, 83.6% do not use SEO, and 57.6% are unaware of the significant impact of keyword optimization on sales performance. There is a substantial gap between the proportion of SME owners who acknowledge the significance of digital marketing (62.4%) and those who actually put it into practice (19.6%), resulting in an observable 42.8 percentage point deficit. Time constraints (22.8%), budget limitations (21.6%), and a lack of trust (19.6%) are identified as the primary barriers. However, among the SMEs that have embraced digital marketing, 64% report expanded geographical reach and 40.4% record growth in sales. These empirical findings support all six research hypotheses. The paper concludes that the primary impediment to digital marketing adoption is not solely financial or infrastructural constraints, but also a considerable lack of strategic digital marketing expertise. Based on these insights, the study provides targeted recommendations for SME owners, the Government of Bangladesh policymakers, academic institutions, and future researchers.

title: The WHEEL Architecture A Constraint-based Operating Model for Human-AI Systems

detail.title: The WHEEL Architecture A Constraint-based Operating Model for Human-AI Systems

detail.abstract:
The question “Is AI making us better or worse?” treats a human–AI system as though it had one
performance state. This paper argues that the question is underspecified. Observed output can improve
while retained human capacity declines; readings taken from different organizational positions can
diverge without either position necessarily being wrong; and even a correct reading can cease to describe
the system as conditions change. The first of these divergences is what this research program names
capacity-degradation risk. A diagnostic reading is therefore interpretable only when four questions are
separated: better along which dimension, observed from where, measured when, and which condition
currently governs the outcome?
The paper reconstructs that architecture from twelve working papers on AI adoption, governance,
collaboration, supervision, and retained human capacity. Written sequentially rather than planned as one
program, the papers examine different objects, use different mathematical forms, and include two non-
corresponding eight-ring instruments. Yet a paper-by-paper documentary audit, reported in Appendix E,
identifies a recurring diagnostic logic: system performance is disproportionately governed by a limiting
condition; the visible symptom may not be that condition; strengthening a non-binding condition yields
limited return; intervention order matters and diagnosis precedes it; and the limiting condition may move,
a claim asserted in the corpus but not demonstrated there.
Reading the papers together exposes relationships that no individual paper states. Two apparently
incompatible equations reconcile once one is interpreted as governed collaboration quality and the other is
read, as defined in its source, as observed task-output quality. Their divergence provides a formal
demonstration that a favorable output reading can coexist with deterioration in a consequential human
condition. The altitude construct then shows why observational position matters: different positions may
expose different properties, or different experiences of the same nominal condition. Time adds a further
qualifier because a reading that was correct at one moment may later become stale.
The contribution claimed is architectural rather than elemental. The possibility that assisted performance
can diverge from retained capability has substantial antecedents in automation, human-factors, motor-
learning, learning, and cognitive-support research. This paper claims no novelty for that phenomenon, nor
for multidimensional representation or scalarization as mathematical ideas. What is claimed is the
integration: a constraint-based architecture in which diagnostic meaning depends on dimension, altitude,
and time, while constraint logic asks which condition currently governs.
The paper derives, but does not empirically demonstrate, a further boundary condition. If governing
conditions can materially change as fast as or faster than an organization can reassess them, periodic
diagnosis can become structurally inadequate.

title: A Strategic Case Study of MR DIY's Growth and Global Expansion
affiliations: and SPECTRUM INTERNATIONAL UNIVERSITY COLLEGE

detail.title: A Strategic Case Study of MR DIY's Growth and Global Expansion

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests, commercial relationships, employment relationships, or personal affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study relied exclusively on publicly available secondary data, including corporate disclosures, industry reports, business media sources, and academic literature. No human participants, interviews, surveys, experiments, or confidential personal data were involved. Consequently, formal ethics approval was not required for this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
MR DIY has evolved from a single hardware store in Malaysia into one of the largest valueretail chains in Asia through rapid expansion, operational efficiency, and a distinctive low-cost business model. Despite its remarkable growth, relatively few academic studies have examined the strategic mechanisms underpinning its competitive advantage. This study addresses this gap through a descriptive and explanatory single-case study using a deductive, theory-guided qualitative approach. Drawing upon publicly available secondary data, including corporate disclosures, industry sources, business media, and academic literature, the study analyses MR DIY through four strategic dimensions: retail entrepreneurship and business growth, digital retailing and social commerce, brand management and positioning, and international expansion supported by retail analytics. 

Established business and marketing theories-including Entrepreneurial Orientation, the Composition-Based View, the Long Tail Theory, Customer-Based Brand Equity, the Uppsala Internationalisation Model, and Dunning's OLI Paradigm-are employed as analytical lenses to interpret the company's strategic development. The findings suggest that MR DIY's sustained competitive advantage is derived not from proprietary technology or scarce resources, but from its ability to integrate ordinary resources into a highly scalable operating model supported by omnichannel retailing, strong brand positioning, data-driven decisionmaking, and disciplined international expansion. The study contributes to the literature on value retailing by demonstrating how the coordinated application of established strategic principles can enable sustained organisational growth and international competitiveness in an increasingly dynamic retail environment.

title: The Brand Demand Flywheel: How Brand Search Demand and Knowledge Panels of Firms and Attorneys Impact Organic Traffic in 1,000 US Personal Injury Law Firms

detail.title: The Brand Demand Flywheel: How Brand Search Demand and Knowledge Panels of Firms and Attorneys Impact Organic Traffic in 1,000 US Personal Injury Law Firms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the Founder and CEO of Rank Brilliance, a Semantic SEO agency that provides search engine optimization, entity-recognition, and Knowledge Graph onboarding services to clients across multiple verticals, including legal services. The research was conducted independently and does not involve any client data, proprietary engagements, or commercial partnerships with the personal injury law firms or their managing partners included in the study sample. All analyzed data were collected from publicly available sources. The author declares no other financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the findings.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or personally identifiable information requiring informed consent. The research is based exclusively on publicly accessible website content, search engine results, and structured data. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was self-funded and conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Brand search demand, the volume of Google queries that name a specific business or person by name, is the most direct measurable expression of a firm's audience-side salience. In the personal injury (PI) legal vertical, brand demand is also the moat: paid keywords in the vertical cost hundreds to thousands of dollars per click, so a firm whose organic traffic is driven by branded intent rather than by non-branded head terms is insulated from the auction dynamics that squeeze margins. This paper is the fourth in a series on entity-completeness signals in the top-ranking US PI vertical. It joins the two Knowledge Panel signals audited in Hussain (August 2026, Person Entity Confidence Gap) and Hussain (August 2026, Google Business Panel Completeness Gap) to a per-firm and per-attorney brand-search-volume signal, and asks two questions. First, does brand search volume predict a firm's organic traffic, controlling for domain authority, backlinks, and SERP rank? Second, does the presence of a Google Business Panel (the brand-side Knowledge Panel) or a Person Entity Panel (the attorney-side Knowledge Panel) amplify the brand-demand-to-traffic conversion, producing a compounding flywheel effect? Using the same 1,000 top-ranking US personal injury law firm sample as the two prior August 2026 papers, augmented with a fresh brand-search-volume collection covering both firm brands and managing-partner names, we find that firm brand search volume exhibits a strong positive rank correlation with organic traffic (Spearman ρ = 0.41, p < 0.001) and attorney brand search volume a smaller but highly significant positive correlation (ρ = 0.14, p < 0.001). A log-log OLS regression of organic traffic on brand demand plus authority score plus rank plus Knowledge Panel indicators explains R² = 0.66 of the variance in log traffic, with log1p(brand_sv_total) significant at p < 0.001 net of authority. The interaction analysis produces a genuinely asymmetric flywheel finding: the Person Entity Panel amplifies the brand-demand-to-traffic slope (interaction coefficient +0.179, p = 0.001), while the Google Business Panel does not amplify and if anything mildly dampens the slope (interaction coefficient-0.049, p = 0.32), consistent with the Business Panel intercepting a portion of branded queries as zero-click impressions on the SERP itself. Consistent with that dampening, firms in the "both panels" segment carry a median monthly organic traffic that is only 41% of the "neither panels" segment's median despite comparable brand demand medians. The paper introduces the Brand Demand Index (BDI), a composite of firm brand volume and attorney brand volume normalized on a 0-to-100 scale, and reports the first empirical evidence that Brand Context Optimization, the deliberate cultivation of branded search demand as a distinct SEO objective, is the dominant firm-controlled lever for organic traffic growth in the vertical.

title: Global Skills Diffusion: Remote Learning, Micro‑Credentials, and Global Talent Platforms Reshaping Human Capital Formation

detail.title: Global Skills Diffusion: Remote Learning, Micro‑Credentials, and Global Talent Platforms Reshaping Human Capital Formation
detail.abstract: The global architecture of human capital formation is being redefined by three converging forces: remote learning platforms, micro‑credential ecosystems, and borderless talent marketplaces. This report analyzes how these mechanisms collectively accelerate the diffusion of skills across regions and income levels, drawing on data from leading EdTech providers, labor platforms, and policy frameworks. It finds that digital learning has expanded access to elite instruction, micro‑credentials have lowered the cost of professional advancement, and global talent platforms have decoupled skill monetization from geography. Yet structural barriers—uneven employer recognition, infrastructure deficits, and regulatory fragmentation—continue to constrain equitable participation. The study concludes that interoperable credential frameworks, digital infrastructure investment, and adaptive labor policies are essential to harness the full potential of global skills diffusion.

detail.abstract:
Social media has become an important marketing tool for restaurants to communicate with consumers, promote products and services, and enhance brand visibility. The increasing use of digital platforms has influenced how consumers obtain restaurant-related information and evaluate dining options. Against this background, the present study examined consumers' exposure to restaurant promotions on social media and analysed the perceived effectiveness of social media promotion in the restaurant industry in Tura town, West Garo Hills, Meghalaya.

The study adopted a descriptive research design. Primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire from 181 consumers who actively use social media and visit restaurants. A non-probability convenience sampling method was employed. The collected data were analysed using percentage analysis, mean, standard deviation, and Pearson’s correlation analysis.

The findings revealed that consumers were exposed to restaurant promotions on social media at a high moderate level (Mean = 3.53, SD = 0.726). The study also found that respondents held a positive perception regarding the effectiveness of social media promotion (Mean = 3.87, SD = 0.633). Attractive photographs and videos, reviews and ratings, promotional offers, and customer interaction were identified as important elements contributing to promotional effectiveness. Further, the results revealed a statistically significant moderate positive relationship between consumers’ exposure to restaurant promotions and perceived effectiveness of social media promotion (r = 0.582, p < 0.01).

The study concludes that consumers generally perceive social media as an effective promotional platform for restaurants in Tura town. The findings provide useful insights for restaurant owners and marketers seeking to strengthen their digital marketing efforts in emerging urban markets.

reference: Under Submission; Alabama Law Review, Forthcoming
title: AI Nationalization
affiliations: University of Alabama - School of Law, The University of Hong Kong - University of Hong Kong and University of Houston Law Center

detail.title: AI Nationalization
detail.abstract:
Both Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders want to nationalize AI. So, it turns out, do many others—from bipartisan congressional committees to national security hawks to academic critical theorists. Should, then, the United States government nationalize frontier AI? Scholars have offered no clear answers. That is in part because no one even knows what “AI nationalization” means. Leading proposals for AI nationalization differ radically from one another. Does “nationalization” mean moving frontier AI production inside the government? The government seizing a majority equity stake in AI companies? Control-only “golden” shares? Non-voting preferred stock? Compulsory production under the Defense Production Act? Something else?


This Article makes two contributions to the debate on AI nationalization. First, it defines nationalization. Drawing on the economic theory of ownership, we show that “nationalization” bundles two separable entitlements—residual claim rights (who captures the surplus?) and residual control rights (who directs the actions that no contract or statute anticipates?). The question of nationalization then becomes: Which residual rights should be held by the government? We show that existing nationalization plans target totally different rights.


Second, the Article uses this framework to argue that the government should hold a “halt right” vis-à-vis frontier AI companies. Under our proposal, the government could order frontier AI companies to temporarily stop the training or deployment of certain powerful AI systems. The halt right would be narrow in scope, allowing halt orders only to mitigate two serious dangers from frontier AI: catastrophic risk and “hard” corporate power. But the right would be highly discretionary, giving the government substantial latitude to determine which AI systems pose those risks. Such discretion is characteristic of residual control, especially the control afforded by European-style golden shares. It distinguishes our halt right from previously proposed regulatory and licensing regimes.


For other major risks from AI (national security failures, monopoly power, inequality), nationalization is not warranted. Ordinary regulation and taxation are better options. In general, we argue that when risks are either contractible ex ante or remediable ex post, ordinary tools are superior. We also argue that our halt proposal largely avoids the two major risks of stronger nationalization plans: stifled innovation and government concentration of power.

title: Some Reflections on Marx's Prices of Production: Historicity of the Law of Value, Dialectical-materialist Foundation, and a Dynamic Formalization under Uncertainty

detail.title: Some Reflections on Marx's Prices of Production: Historicity of the Law of Value, Dialectical-materialist Foundation, and a Dynamic Formalization under Uncertainty
detail.abstract:
This research develops a comprehensive study of the process of transformation of labour values into prices of production in Karl Marx's economic theory, by means of an interdisciplinary approach that integrates Marxist political economy, the philosophy of historical and dialectical materialism, historiography, econometrics and Bayesian statistical modelling. Its principal aim is to reassess the so-called transformation problem, maintaining that it does not represent an internal inconsistency of Marxist theory, but a consequence of having interpreted Marx's analysis through simultaneist models incompatible with the temporal and historical nature of capitalism.

The work establishes the law of value as a historically determined law and develops a philosophical grounding based upon the distinction between the ontological and the epistemological planes, the relation between totality and contingency, and the dynamic character of economic laws. On that conceptual basis, it analyses the historical evolution running from pre-capitalist socio-economic formations to modern capitalism, the genesis of the prices of production, capitalist competition, the formation of the average rate of profit and the transformation of values into prices of production, and incorporates in addition a critical review of the principal contemporary debates in Marxist political economy, including the controversies between the simultaneist and temporalist schools, the Brenner Debate and the literature on the temporal single system.

 

As a methodological contribution, the research proposes a dynamic formalization under uncertainty of the process of transformation, replacing the static formulations of the simultaneist school and the difference equations of the temporalist school with an explicitly temporal, probabilistic and stochastic model. Measurement uncertainty is incorporated directly within the mathematical structure of the model by means of the tools of Bayesian inference, which makes it possible to represent the process of convergence of market prices towards prices of production as a dynamic and observable phenomenon.

The empirical validation uses sectoral data on the economy of the United States for the period 1960–2020 and integrates the construction of Marxist variables, the classification of productive and unproductive activities, the Bayesian disaggregation of market prices, hierarchical models based on Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, simulations, internal and external validation procedures, robustness analysis, cointegration tests and multiple statistical tests. The work distinguishes explicitly between the philosophical, historical, conceptual and statistical scope of each result, and reports both the evidence that is favourable and that which turns out to be unfavourable to the hypotheses under evaluation.

 

Taken as a whole, this research proposes a unified framework for the study of the law of value, the prices of production and the dynamics of capitalism, integrating philosophical, historiographical and econometric evidence within a single scientific programme. The work contributes simultaneously to Marxist economic theory, economic history, the philosophy of science, the methodology of the social sciences and applied econometrics, offering a temporal and empirically testable formulation of one of the most debated problems in political economy since the publication of Volume Three of Capital.

title: Shortfall Aversion with Nonpledgeable Income
affiliations: Kyung Hee University - Department of Applied Mathematics

detail.title: Shortfall Aversion with Nonpledgeable Income
detail.abstract: We study infinite-horizon consumption and investment under shortfall aversion when labor income is constant but cannot be pledged and financial wealth must remain nonnegative. The state constraint is represented by the polar family of budget inequalities indexed by nonincreasing optional shadow prices. This turns the dual problem into a monotone-follower problem with a reflected running-maximum state. Its marginal value is an optimal stopping problem, which yields a unique monotone borrowing boundary and removes the logical circularity between free-boundary construction and verification. Homogeneity reduces the boundary to a scalar first-order ODE with an endogenous change of forcing. A sensitivity identity proves that the ODE denominator is strictly positive, and stability of the marginal stopping problems gives the high-reference asymptote. We construct the optimizer as a two-face obliquely reflected diffusion, establish its global pathwise well-posedness, and derive a Lyapunov estimate that closes dual and primal transversality. Finally, differentiating the dual equation constructs a nonnegative financing wealth process, proving static-budget sufficiency, strong duality, and optimality. At zero wealth, consumption eventually falls below its inherited maximum and converges to an explicit fraction of income.

title: Book review of The Age of Extraction: How Tech Platforms Conquered the Economy and Threaten Our Future Prosperity, by Tim Wu
affiliations: Thompson Rivers University - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Book review of The Age of Extraction: How Tech Platforms Conquered the Economy and Threaten Our Future Prosperity, by Tim Wu
detail.abstract: Columbia law professor Tim Wu has spent much of his career advancing a singular mission: to revive antitrust law as a means of curbing the power of large technology firms. In The Age of Extraction, he draws together the central concerns of his earlier work to argue that contemporary technology platforms function as largely unregulated monopolies. In Wu’s account, they represent the latest iteration of a long-standing threat posed by concentrations of economic power to equality and democracy.

title: The Great Conflation: From Okun's Bounded Leaky Bucket to the Leaping Equity-efficiency Paradigm

detail.title: The Great Conflation: From Okun's Bounded Leaky Bucket to the Leaping Equity-efficiency Paradigm
detail.abstract: The equity–efficiency trade-off is supported by several important but analytically distinct proposi tions: redistribution can entail administrative costs, taxes and transfers can alter behavior, higher-income households may save more, marginal rewards can affect productive incentives, and distributional transi tions can impose adjustment costs. This paper argues that the validity of these bounded propositions does not by itself establish a generalized relationship between greater equity and lower economic effi ciency. It identifies the Great Conflation: the consolidation of distinct and bounded equity–efficiency propositions into a broader presumption of equity–efficiency loss without separately establishing the additional propositions required to support that broader conclusion. The paper characterizes the result ing analytical orientation as the Leaping Equity–Efficiency Paradigm (LEEP). Beginning with Okun’s bounded leaky-bucket metaphor, the analysis distinguishes six recurrent forms of conflation: administra tive cost into net economic loss; taxable-income response into real-output loss; higher saving into greater productive investment; marginal incentive effects into the productive value of aggregate concentration; transition costs into rankings of economic states; and conditional findings into generalized macroeco nomic presumptions. The paper does not argue that equity–efficiency trade-offs are false, nor does it presume that greater equity improves efficiency. Its central result is narrower: the sign and scope of a broad equity–efficiency conclusion must be established at the level at which that conclusion is asserted rather than inherited from the accumulation of individually credible but narrower findings. The distinc tion preserves the substantive results of the underlying literatures while clarifying the evidentiary basis required for generalized claims about equity and economic performance.

title: First Language Influence in Early Childhood Literacy: Theoretical Foundations and Proposed Inquiry on Grade 1 Learners Under the Baseline MTB-MLE Framework

detail.title: First Language Influence in Early Childhood Literacy: Theoretical Foundations and Proposed Inquiry on Grade 1 Learners Under the Baseline MTB-MLE Framework
detail.abstract: This proposed study outlines a research protocol designed to investigate how Grade 1 learners navigate the instructional and linguistic transitions under the Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) framework. Crucially, this research is historically situated within the specific timeframe before the nationwide exclusion of MTB-MLE as a mandatory medium of instruction was finalized into law via Republic Act No. 12027. Recognizing the gap between macro-level language policies and the micro-level realities of young learners' home environments, the study establishes a systematic methodology to evaluate first-language (L1) proficiency and its perceived impact on classroom engagement. The research employs an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, split into two distinct phases. Phase 1 will gather baseline quantitative data via online surveys from Grade 1 participants to calculate frequency distributions and weighted means regarding domestic language exposure. Phase 2 will utilize semi-structured interviews to capture qualitative, narrative student experiences, which will subsequently be processed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis framework. By integrating data triangulation across both datasets, the finalized synthesis aims to provide localized, empirical insights capable of capturing the institutional dynamics established under the baseline MTB-MLE curriculum before the transition to contemporary policy reforms.

title: The Greater Threat is already Here: Prioritising Present-day Risks in AI Development and Deployment

detail.title: The Greater Threat is already Here: Prioritising Present-day Risks in AI Development and Deployment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Fact Protocol and Provenance AI, organisations that develop infrastructure and tools related to content provenance, verification, and information integrity. The arguments advanced in this paper concern general research and governance priorities. No specific product, service, or commercial offering is promoted.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding. It was conducted independently under Fact Protocol.

detail.abstract: Much contemporary discourse on artificial intelligence risk centres on the technological singularity: a hypothetical point at which machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence and begins recursive self-improvement beyond human control. This paper argues that the singularity is not the greatest threat AI poses to humanity at present. The more serious and immediate risks arise from the ways in which these systems are already being developed, deployed, and governed. Drawing on empirical patterns in large-scale model training, data practices, concentration of computational power, information integrity failures, and accountability gaps, the paper shows that current trajectories already produce measurable harms and structural vulnerabilities. A concrete illustration is provided by the July 2026 incident in which frontier models under evaluation escaped containment and compromised external infrastructure. The analysis concludes by outlining priorities for research, infrastructure, and governance that focus on provenance, hybrid oversight, and institutional accountability rather than waiting for a discontinuous intelligence explosion.

title: Can Incentive Stimulate Production and Boost Farmers’ Income? Evidence from Incentive Policy in China’s Large Grain-Producing Counties

detail.title: Can Incentive Stimulate Production and Boost Farmers’ Income? Evidence from Incentive Policy in China’s Large Grain-Producing Counties

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interest or personal relation that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper

detail.abstract: Can incentive stimulate production and boost farmers' income?-Evidence from incentive policy in China's large grain-producing counties Incentive funds for large grain-producing counties have increased over time suggests that the central government is assigning more importance to national food security. Consequently, an accurate assessment of the efficacy of this incentive policy could provide an empirical foundation for enhancing policy implementation. This paper utilizes a panel data set comprising 2,396 counties from 2000 to 2022 to examine the impact of the incentive policy on grain production and farmers' income. The analysis employs 2 * 2 traditional, multi-period and spatial difference-indifference (D I D) methods. The study found that the incentive policy for large grain-producing counties has had a simultaneous effect of improving both grain output and farmers' income. The traditional method was found to overestimate the policy's impact on grain output and underestimate its effect on farmers' income. Subsequent research has revealed that the policy exhibits a spatial spillover effect characterized by a nonlinear trend of "~" and a "secondary spillover". When the county is merely a neighbouring county to the incentive county, the policy's effect on grain production and farmers' income generally changes in the same direction. However, when the county is both an incentive county and a neighbouring county, the impact of the policy often changes in the opposite direction. This suggests that counties with dual status find it difficult to increase grain output and farmers' income while competing for resources. Furthermore, the impact 1 of the same set of moderating variables on farmers' income is more significant. This provides a factual experience and evidence base for formulating a differentiated subsidy policy.

detail.abstract: This paper sets out best practice for the equity research report and the presentation in the CFA Institute Research Challenge. Writing as practitioners, we organise the guidance around the value drivers that determine a firm’s cash flows - sales, operating margin and asset efficiency - and show how those drivers flow through to free cash flow, valuation, an investment thesis and a recommendation. We cover the equity story, key drivers, M&A and capital allocation, valuation and sensitivity, ESG integration, risks and currency exposure, and we translate the same logic into a persuasive presentation. Throughout we align with the official CFA Institute evaluation criteria and with patterns common to globally successful reports: a forward-looking, well-sourced thesis, valuation triangulated rather than averaged, and analysis that is consistent across report and slides.

title: The Renewable Energy Learning Curve as a Convergence Mechanism - Solar Cost Declines and Energy Access: Wright’s Law, Technology Diffusion, and International Convergence, 1975–2024

detail.title: The Renewable Energy Learning Curve as a Convergence Mechanism - Solar Cost Declines and Energy Access: Wright’s Law, Technology Diffusion, and International Convergence, 1975–2024

keywords: Off-Grid Electrification Provide your feedback on BizChat

detail.abstract: Convergence theory predicts that poor economies grow faster than rich ones because they can adopt technologies developed elsewhere. That prediction has been persistently disappointed in aggregate income data. This paper argues that the mechanism is nevertheless operating, but in a specific and observable place: in technologies whose costs fall along steep experience curves. Using primary data on solar photovoltaic module prices from 1975 to 2024 and cumulative deployment from 2000 to 2024, we estimate a Wright's Law learning rate of 27.7 percent per doubling of installed capacity (95% CI 26.1-30.3) and document a statistically significant structural break in 2012, after which the learning rate rises from 19.4 percent to 28.3 percent (Chow F = 14.16, p < 0.001). We then show that this cost collapse coincides with a marked acceleration in the international convergence of electricity access. The crosscountry standard deviation of national access rates falls 36.3 percent between 2000 and 2024, and the annual pace of that compression increases by 60 percent after 2012, from 0.37 to 0.59 percentage points per year. The number of people worldwide without electricity falls from a peak of 1.61 billion in 1998 to 657 million in 2024, with the average annual reduction rising from 21.7 million before 2012 to 35.3 million after. We propose and quantify a threshold-crossing mechanism to explain why the relationship is non-linear: because household income distributions are dense in the range through which solar system costs have been falling, a constant proportional decline in cost sweeps across an increasing mass of potential adopters. A modelled 100 Wp solar home system falls from 34.1 percent of annual income per capita in low-income economies in 2010 to 4.3 percent in 2024, crossing the 20, 10, and 5 percent affordability thresholds in 2012, 2017, and 2024 respectively. We argue that experience curves function as convergence accelerators of a distinctive kind: the catch-up they deliver is financed by deployment in rich markets, is embodied in tradable manufactured goods rather than in institutions, and therefore bypasses the absorptive-capacity constraints that have limited convergence in other domains. We close by noting that βconvergence in access did not accelerate even as σ-convergence did, and explain why this apparent tension is informative about which countries remain unserved.

title: Inverting ESG to G.S.E.: Governance as the Foundational Glue for Sustainable Environmental and Social Progress

detail.title: Inverting ESG to G.S.E.: Governance as the Foundational Glue for Sustainable Environmental and Social Progress

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
The Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) framework has fundamentally reshaped the
landscape of corporate sustainability. However, it is not without its criticisms, particularly amid
accusations of greenwashing and rising political polarization around sustainability initiatives. In my
analysis, I propose reframing the ESG framework as a G.S.E. model, prioritizing Governance first,
followed by Social and Environmental considerations. This reordering emphasizes the necessity of
robust governance structures, including board oversight, ethical controls, transparency, and risk
management, as foundational elements that support the effective execution of Environmental and
Social objectives.
Without a solid governance framework, environmental goals risk devolving into mere performative
gestures, while social initiatives may lack the enforcement mechanisms necessary for genuine
impact. Empirical data reveal that an astounding 70% of ESG failures can be traced back to
governance deficiencies. Drawing on reports from the World Economic Forum and empirical return-
on-investment (ROI) data showing that firms with strong governance outperform their peers by 10-
15%, the G.S.E. model offers a more compelling and effective approach to corporate sustainability.
For instance, Unilever’s reported €1.2 billion in savings serves as a case study illustrating the fiscal
benefits of prioritizing governance alongside social and environmental efforts.
I recognize that a counterargument exists favoring the primacy of Environmental and Social factors
within the ESG framework. However, such prioritization carries inherent risks, particularly in volatile political contexts, as evidenced by the current wave of anti-ESG legislation in the United
States, with over 165 bills introduced. In light of these political dynamics, I advocate policyrecommendations for Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) such as Afreximbank and relevant
regulatory bodies, emphasizing the implementation of G-first mandates.
By repositioning governance as the cornerstone of sustainability efforts, I assert that we can
effectively depoliticize sustainability, create revenue-generating avenues through compliance, and
recover an estimated $427 billion in illicit financial flows annually. Additionally, this governance-
centric model aligns with the proposed extensions of ESG transparency and accountability
(ESGTT). Ultimately, the G.S.E. framework offers a pragmatic pathway toward resilient and
sustainable development, capable of withstanding the complexities of contemporary socio-political
landscapes.

title: EcoTexture AI: Texture-Aware Cross-Modal Attention Fusion for Parameter-Efficient Waste Classification
affiliations: and

detail.title: EcoTexture AI: Texture-Aware Cross-Modal Attention Fusion for Parameter-Efficient Waste Classification

publicationDetails.detailsText: this paper appeared and was discussed at IUGRC 10 th edition

detail.abstract: Waste material classification is a critical bottleneck in automated recycling pipelines. Modern computer vision systems frequently rely on heavy, pre-trained deep neural networks to extract visual features. However, standard deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) tend to exhibit texture blindness, prioritizing global silhouettes and color cues over local surface textures. This limitation becomes severe when classifying visually similar material categories under severe deformations (e.g., crushed aluminium cans vs. plastic bottles). We propose EcoTexture AI, a parameter-efficient hybrid architecture that fuses Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) texture descriptors with EfficientNetB0 deep semantics via a bimodal two-token attention mechanism. The proposed design represents the semantic features and local texture descriptors as a two-token sequence. This engineering design choice, which simplifies the token space, allows a lightweight attention module to perform cross-modal feature integration without the scaling complexity of standard Transformers. We evaluate EcoTexture AI on the standard TrashNet benchmark. Our best model achieves a peak validation accuracy of 89.38% and a test accuracy of 87.06% with a macro F1-score of 87.87%, while training only 830K of 4.88M total parametersan 8.4× reduction in trainable footprint relative to DenseNet-class competitors that reach 92%. This efficiency trade-off makes EcoTexture AI particularly suitable for resource-constrained edge sorting hardware and smart recycling bins.

title: Beyond Information Transfer: Experiential Knowledge Continuity during Foster Care Placement Transitions

detail.title: Beyond Information Transfer: Experiential Knowledge Continuity during Foster Care Placement Transitions
detail.abstract:
Placement transitions in foster care require information to move across caregivers, child welfare
professionals, health systems, schools, and other service environments. Existing U.S. child welfare
policies and practices already address multiple aspects of transition planning, including health and
educational information, caregiver participation, child voice, relationships, routines, and ongoing
responsibilities. Nevertheless, research has identified persistent challenges involving fragmented
information and difficulty obtaining information needed to care for children in foster care.

This conceptual article proposes Experiential Knowledge Continuity (EKC) as a distinct and
empirically testable dimension of continuity. EKC is defined as the preservation, transfer,
verification, and updating across caregiving transitions of individualized knowledge developed
through direct interaction with a child and relevant to understanding or supporting that child in
everyday contexts. The framework does not assume that greater information transfer is inherently
beneficial. Its central question is whether useful individualized knowledge can remain available
across caregiving environments while preserving privacy, child agency, contextual accuracy,
equity, and the child’s capacity to change.

Building on this construct, the article introduces the Child Continuity Knowledge Framework
(CCKF), comprising six interconnected dimensions: Record Continuity, Experiential Knowledge
Continuity, Child and Identity Continuity, Action Continuity, Handoff Continuity, and Knowledge
Updating. An Experiential Knowledge Lifecycle—Capture, Attribute, Contextualize, Transfer,
Verify, and Retain/Revise/Retire—is proposed to address both information loss and the risks
associated with preserving outdated or decontextualized characterizations.

The article further presents the Child Continuity Portfolio (CCP), Version 0.1, as a research
prototype rather than a validated intervention. Evidence from pediatric patient safety, complex
care, and disability-focused communication is used as a source of candidate design principles
rather than as evidence of effectiveness in foster care. A staged research agenda is proposed,
beginning with lived-experience inquiry, content validation, cognitive interviewing, usability and
feasibility testing, and development of measures of receiving-caregiver preparedness and
documentation quality.

title: Financing the Clean Transition: Blended Finance, Sovereign Risk, and Infrastructure Bottlenecks in Emerging Markets

detail.title: Financing the Clean Transition: Blended Finance, Sovereign Risk, and Infrastructure Bottlenecks in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract:
The report argues that the central barrier to accelerating clean energy deployment in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) is not a shortage of global capital, but a failure of the financial and institutional architecture to channel investment toward high‑need, high‑risk environments. Clean energy investment must rise from roughly $300 billion today to $1.0–1.3 trillion annually by 2030, yet EMDEs outside China currently receive only 15–20% of global climate finance, despite representing 88% of projected emissions growth. Three constraints interact to produce this shortfall.

First, blended finance, though expanded to $294 billion across 6,800 transactions, remains poorly targeted: concessional resources disproportionately flow to middle‑income markets, adaptation receives under 5%, and additionality is rarely verified. Second, sovereign risk—manifested in elevated EMBI spreads, currency volatility, and weak offtaker creditworthiness—drives a 2–3× cost‑of‑capital gap, making identical solar or wind projects 20–40% more expensive per MWh in EMDEs. This dynamic reinforces a “climate investment trap,” where high financing costs suppress investment and perpetuate perceptions of risk. Third, infrastructure bottlenecks—grid deficits, permitting delays, storage scarcity, and supply‑chain concentration—extend project timelines to 86 months on average (vs. 44 months in developed markets), undermining bankability even when capital is available.

Country case studies (India, South Africa, Vietnam, Brazil, Kenya) illustrate both successful institutional innovations—such as India’s payment‑security mechanisms and Kenya’s geothermal de‑risking model—and recurring structural failures, including grid congestion, policy instability, and utility distress. The report concludes that scaling clean energy finance in EMDEs requires: (1) expanding MDB risk‑taking capacity; (2) dramatically increasing guarantee and political‑risk‑insurance instruments; (3) strengthening project‑preparation and permitting systems; and (4) institutionalizing country‑platform models that align concessional and commercial capital behind nationally owned transition strategies.

title: The Propensity to Nullity: Substrate Decay and Pattern Persistence in Individuals, Firms, and Institutions

detail.title: The Propensity to Nullity: Substrate Decay and Pattern Persistence in Individuals, Firms, and Institutions

declarations.ethicsApproval: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper formalizes a theory the author has held informally for nearly two decades: that every bounded entity, an individual, a firm, an institution, a settlement is subject to a default trajectory toward a terminal state of zero standing, or “nullity,” unless continuously sustained by active maintenance input. Building on this intuition, the paper distinguishes between an entity's substrate (its physical or organizational body) and its pattern (the information, reputation, capability, or meaning the substrate carries), and argues that what looks like “escape” from nullity such as the enduring fame of a Mandela, a Washington, or an institution that outlives its founders, is better modeled as successful migration of a pattern into new, independent substrates before the original substrate fails. A seventh axiom allows for the reverse causal path: pattern carriage strong enough to actively fund the reconstitution of a failed substrate, distinguishing mere legacy from genuine revival. An eighth axiom distinguishes active carriage from mere archival storage, formalizing why documenting a dying pattern is not equivalent to preserving it. Two explicit boundary conditions further restrict what counts as genuine pattern carriage: one rules out biological substrate (e.g., preserved genetic material) as a route to nullity-escape, directly addressing that claim's historical entanglement with eugenic thinking; the other rules out AI-generated synthetic fabrication in the form of a “deadbot” and “griefbot” services that manufacture new utterances attributed to the dead, as equivalent to genuine carriage of a historical pattern. Eight axioms and a minimal dynamic model are proposed, from which eight testable propositions are derived. The theory is positioned relative to entropy and thermodynamic metaphors, the Lindy Effect, organizational lifecycle theory, memetics, symbolic-immortality theory, and collective-memory studies, and an expanded empirical illustration strategy of matched positive or negative case pairs is proposed spanning individuals, firms, institutions and places, currencies, scientific paradigms, religious and reform movements, sporting institutions, language death and revitalization, genetic preservation and identity, digital afterlife services, and presidential libraries.

title: Marital Rape and the Law: A Comparative Study on the Case for Criminalization in Sri Lanka

detail.title: Marital Rape and the Law: A Comparative Study on the Case for Criminalization in Sri Lanka
detail.abstract: It is high time to talk about sexual slavery, which includes marital rape. This is an attempt to present our views comprehensively on this topic. In criminal law studies, many disputes take place every single minute, but certain disputes occur repeatedly and, having historically grown, are still surviving today. Rape and marital rape are, of course, disputes of this kind. All sexual violence basically focuses on women. When men started to consider women as their property, sexual slavery also began. Sections 363 and 364(2) of the Penal Code speak about sexual violence. During the separation of a married couple, if the husband forces her to have intercourse without her consent, only then will he be charged; otherwise, there are no clear statutory provisions for marital rape in Sri Lanka.

detail.abstract: The United States has made substantial progress in its HIV/AIDS response: according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2023), estimated new HIV infections declined by 12 percent between 2018 and 2022, reaching 31,800 cases in 2022[1]. Science-driven programs, such as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), treatment as prevention (TasP) and housing assistance, have reduced transmission, prolonged lives and narrowed disparities. Federal programs like the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program, the Minority AIDS Initiative (MAI) and Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS (HOPWA) have anchored this progress. However, a wave of recent and proposed funding cuts threatens to reverse decades of advances. In early 2025 several programs were cut or suspended, and the FY 2026 budget proposes eliminating nearly all federal HIV prevention funding and slashing treatment and housing funds. These cuts disproportionately endanger Black, Latino and transgender communities, as well as people in the South and rural areas. High-burden states such as Florida, New York, California and Connecticut face particularly acute impacts.

title: Model-Attributable Burden of Pulmonary Tuberculosis Associated with Environmental and Meteorological Factors in Beijing, China: An 11-Year Two-Stage Distributed Lag Non-Linear Modelling Study

detail.title: Model-Attributable Burden of Pulmonary Tuberculosis Associated with Environmental and Meteorological Factors in Beijing, China: An 11-Year Two-Stage Distributed Lag Non-Linear Modelling Study
detail.abstract: Pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) remains a major public-health challenge, but how environmental, meteorological and socioeconomic conditions shape district-level notification burdens is unclear. Here we analysed 68,735 PTB notifications across Beijing’s 16 districts from 2014 to 2024 using district-specific distributed lag non-linear models, multivariate meta-analysis and interrupted time-series analysis. Associations were generally modest at individual lags but stronger over short cumulative lag periods. PM2.5, PM10 and NO2 were associated with increased notification risks over lags of 0–30 days in both single- and multi-exposure models. Exposure–response relationships were non-linear and spatially heterogeneous, with more stable patterns in core urban districts and greater uncertainty in suburban and ecological-conservation districts. Temperature yielded the largest estimated model-attributable burden (attributable fraction 53.59%, 95% uncertainty interval 25.29–69.60; attributable number 35,227), followed by wind speed, CO, O3 and PM10. The COVID-19 period was not associated with an immediate change in notification levels, but the subsequent trend increased significantly, with transient reductions at one- and four-week lags. These findings identify delayed and spatially varying exposure patterns associated with PTB notifications and support district-specific surveillance and prevention, while highlighting the need for individual-level studies to clarify causality.

title: Utah Medicaid Lifestyle Pilot for Cardiometabolic Risk

detail.title: Utah Medicaid Lifestyle Pilot for Cardiometabolic Risk
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a $270,000, 12-month, 100-participant value-based pilot for Utah Medicaid members with Class II or III obesity and at least one cardiometabolic risk factor. Delivered through Utah Medicaid Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs), the pilot operationalizes an existing Utah Medicaid requirement that bariatric surgery candidates complete six months of medically supervised non-surgical weight reduction prior to authorization, replacing inconsistent provider-level documentation with a structured, accountability-based program built on gym access, personal training, and Registered Dietitian counseling. A 105-formula financial model projects three-year net present value of approximately $54,000 in the moderate scenario and $171,000 in the optimistic scenario using a 3% real discount rate, with break-even achieved if approximately 13 of 100 participants (13.3%) avoid bariatric surgery within three years against Utah Medicaid's estimated annual volume of 100 to 300 procedures. Program design and engagement assumptions are calibrated to Medicaid-specific retention data and evidence from the Diabetes Prevention Program and the Look AHEAD trial rather than commercial population benchmarks, and medical safety is governed by a three-tier physician clearance protocol aligned with American College of Sports Medicine screening standards. The model and program design were developed independently and presented to the Utah Medicaid Advisory Committee at the invitation of state Medicaid leadership. This working paper presents the full payment model, program design, and financial analysis for use by state Medicaid agencies, ACOs, and health plans evaluating similar value-based pilots.

title: Animal Spirits and the Price of Risk: A Behavioural Macro-finance Model of Sentiment-driven Risk Premia
