The views and empirical findings expressed in this paper are strictly those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official position of their affiliated academic or non-governmental institutions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical clearance for primary data collection was guided by institutional academic standards at Khulna University. Informed verbal consent was obtained from all individual respondents prior to conducting household interviews. Participants were informed about the voluntary nature of participation, data confidentiality and that anonymized data would be used strictly for research purposes.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was conducted with academic support from the Economics Discipline, Khulna University, Bangladesh.

detail.abstract: This study examines association between remittance receipt and agricultural technology adoption at the household level in Shyamnagar Upazila. Ramjannagar union is a climate vulnerable coastal zone of the southwest region of Bangladesh. Agriculture of Ramjannagar faces different challenges due to salinity intrusion, climate variability and limited access to capital. Those challenges make adoption of resilient technologies essential for sustainable production, livelihood and food security. Existing literature shows the role of remittance positively by relaxing liquidity constraints. But empirical evidence of remittance association with technology adoption remains limited particularly in coastal Bangladesh. This study constructs a Technology Adoption Index (TAI) based on 18 resilient agricultural practices using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with different determinants of TAI in Ramjannagar union. Remittance receipt may be endogenous. So, the study estimates an OLS model as the baseline specification and employs instrumental-variable two-stage least squares (2SLS) as a robustness check. The Durbin-Wu-Hausman test is subsequently used to assess whether remittance is statistically endogenous. Distance to remittance hub is used as instrumental variable to include exogenous variation in remittance. But Hausman test shows remittance is not endogenous. The empirical OLS findings reveal remittance insignificantly associated with technology adoption. Moreover, the association is negative. The inverse direction and magnitude may arise due to salinity, heatwave, waterlog, investment capacity and labor loss effects. However, farming experience, cultivable land size, assets, market distance, age, religion and institutional access are significantly associated with technology adoption.

title: Artificial Intelligence And Data-Driven Computing For Secure And Networked Information Systems: A Comprehensive Review
affiliations: Cosendai Adventist University, University of Ngaoundéré and Independent

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence And Data-Driven Computing For Secure And Networked Information Systems: A Comprehensive Review
detail.abstract: The proliferation of interconnected systems and growth in data generation have transformed information security landscapes, necessitating transition from traditional defensive mechanisms toward intelligent, adaptive architectures. This review systematically examines the convergence of artificial intelligence and data-driven computing in securing modern networked information systems, synthesizing findings from over 500 peer-reviewed publications spanning 2018 through 2025. The analysis presents a taxonomical framework categorizing AI-driven security mechanisms across three dimensions: threat detection and prevention capabilities, privacy-preserving computational methods, and intelligent network management systems. Quantitative evaluation reveals that deep learning approaches achieve detection accuracies exceeding 95% with false positive rates below 5% in controlled environments, yet current defense mechanisms remain effective against only 60% of sophisticated evasion attacks. Federated learning and homomorphic encryption enable privacy preservation, though computational overhead typically introduces latency increases ranging from 2× to 3× in real-time applications. Research gaps persist in adversarial robustness, cross-domain generalization, formal verification of AI security systems, and development of standardized evaluation metrics. This review provides practitioners with evidence-based frameworks for technology selection and deployment strategies while establishing a research agenda addressing challenges in creating resilient, scalable, and trustworthy AI-driven security systems for next-generation networked infrastructures.

title: ESG Risks and Private Equity Returns: New International Evidence
affiliations: University of Hamburg, , University of South Carolina - Moore School of Business, Goethe University Frankfurt, House of Finance (HoF), Graduate School of Economics, Finance and Management (GSEFM), Students and Syracuse University - Whitman School of Management

detail.title: ESG Risks and Private Equity Returns: New International Evidence
detail.abstract: Using a global sample of 23,563 privately held companies owned by 1,465 private equity funds, we document a robust negative relationship between exposure to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) risks through their invested portfolio companies and fund returns. While this relationship challenges the traditional finance axiom that returns compensate for risk, we interpret our findings as a normative penalty based on institutional theory. ESG risks are not just ethical concerns. Rather, exposure to ESG risks is genuinely bad for investment returns, largely because society increasingly punishes companies that ignore them. Results from moderation analysis show that early-stage venture firms and firms facing liability of foreignness depend more on normative legitimacy, resulting in a higher return penalty. There are also important substitution effects. Later-stage buyout companies are less vulnerable to normative sanctioning because of their higher cognitive legitimacy, and firms in countries with good formal ESG institutions are less vulnerable because of their higher regulative legitimacy. Similarly, stakeholder selection reduces the importance of normative evaluation in sin sector investments. Finally, as more resources become available, normative pressure to conform to ESG institutions strengthens, exacerbating the return penalty. Our study provides valuable practical insights.

title: Responsible Leadership and Financial Flexibility: The Protective Role of Ethical Governance on Debt Capacity During Periods of Economic Uncertainty

detail.title: Responsible Leadership and Financial Flexibility: The Protective Role of Ethical Governance on Debt Capacity During Periods of Economic Uncertainty

detail.abstract: This study examines whether the multi dimensional behaviors of responsible leadership translate into macro level financial resilience by expanding an enterprise's external borrowing capacity and mitigating bankruptcy threats during periods of systemic economic uncertainty. Integrating Stakeholder Theory with Agency Theory, we theorize that ethical governance functions as the proximal organizational mechanism through which responsible leadership signals lower default risk to capital providers, thereby enlarging debt capacity and financial flexibility. Drawing on a multi source sample of 438 senior executives and credit risk officers across publicly listed firms in cyclical and defensive industries, we employ a two step Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) procedure incorporating Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and latent moderated mediation analysis. The findings indicate that responsible leadership exerts a significant positive effect on ethical governance quality (β = 0.512, p < .001), which in turn significantly expands debt capacity and financial flexibility (β = 0.401, p < .001) and reduces bankruptcy threat (β =-.358, p < .001). Economic uncertainty significantly strengthens the indirect pathway (index of moderated mediation = 0.131, 95% CI [0.072, 0.198]), such that the protective role of ethical governance intensifies precisely when systemic shocks are most severe. The study advances stakeholder agency theorizing and offers actionable guidance for boards, CFOs, and credit rating stakeholders navigating turbulent capital markets.

title: The Nexus of Economic Climate and Organizational Behavior: Corporate Sustainability Commitments as a Moderator in the Employee Engagement Firm Value (Tobin's Q) Link During Macroeconomic Contractions

detail.title: The Nexus of Economic Climate and Organizational Behavior: Corporate Sustainability Commitments as a Moderator in the Employee Engagement Firm Value (Tobin's Q) Link During Macroeconomic Contractions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, financial, or organizational conflicts of interest that could have inappropriately influenced or biased the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This study models the micro-macro interface by examining how macroeconomic contractions transmit through the workforce to firm value, and whether corporate sustainability commitments function as an internal stabilizing mechanism that buffers this transmission. Integrating Conservation of Resources theory with Social Exchange Theory and signaling logic, we theorize that economic contraction depresses employee engagement, that engagement in turn sustains market valuation as measured by Tobin's Q, and that credible environmental and social commitments attenuate the erosive effect of economic anxiety on engagement. Drawing on a two wave, multi source sample of 461 employees and senior managers across publicly listed firms, matched with archival valuation data, we employ a two step Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) procedure incorporating Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and latent moderated mediation analysis. The findings indicate that economic contraction significantly reduces employee engagement (β = .443, p < .001), that engagement significantly elevates Tobin's Q (β = .389, p < .001), and that the indirect erosion of firm value through engagement is significant. Corporate sustainability commitments significantly buffer the first stage pathway (index of moderated mediation = 0.118, 95% CI [0.063, 0.179]), such that the protective effect intensifies precisely when economic anxiety is most acute. The study advances micro foundational theorizing of firm value and offers actionable guidance for executives navigating recessions.

title: Competition vs. Sector-specific Regulation in the Digital Space: Old Wine in New Bottles?
affiliations: Tilburg Law and Economics Center (TILEC) and Leiden University, Leiden Law School, Europa Institute

detail.title: Competition vs. Sector-specific Regulation in the Digital Space: Old Wine in New Bottles?
detail.abstract: The debate over the respective merits of competition law and sector-specific regulation in controlling market power is not a new one: it shaped the liberalisation of Europe's network industries, and of telecommunications in particular, more than three decades ago. This chapter revisits that debate in the context of digital markets and of the Digital Markets Act (DMA). It first recalls why competition rules were considered insufficient to open markets dominated by entrenched State monopolies, and what the resulting regulatory frameworks did and did not achieve. It then shows that, although the sources of market power differ-gatekeepers owe their position to first-mover advantages and network effects rather than to exclusive rights granted by the State-the concerns that motivated the DMA closely echo those earlier discussions: control of bottleneck infrastructure, vertical integration and self-preferencing, and exploitative conduct. The chapter argues that the DMA nonetheless represents a new specimen of sector-specific regulation. Its choice of a regulation rather than a directive, its narrow and largely quantitative personal scope, its adjustable obligations, and its centralised public enforcement combined with a private enforcement route make it nimbler and more future-proof than the frameworks adopted for network industries, which have struggled to adapt to new market realities. Situating the DMA within Hancher and Moran's concept of regulatory space, the chapter concludes by identifying the conditions under which its potential can be realised: a genuine yet strict regulatory dialogue, severe sanctions for systematic non-compliance, the active involvement of national competition authorities, the facilitation of private enforcement, and full use of the DMA's capacity for adjustment.

title: Generative AI Integration and Corporate Cash Policies: The Impact of Deployment Intensity on Free Cash Flow Management and Liquidity Buffers

detail.title: Generative AI Integration and Corporate Cash Policies: The Impact of Deployment Intensity on Free Cash Flow Management and Liquidity Buffers

detail.abstract: This study bridges micro level technological deployment dynamics and macro level corporate financial policy by examining how the intensity of generative artificial intelligence integration reshapes free cash flow (FCF) management and optimal liquidity buffers within early adopter firms. Anchored in the Resource Based View (RBV) and the dynamic capabilities perspective, we theorize that the internal velocity of GenAI deployment functions as a higher order organizational capability that enhances working capital forecasting precision, thereby attenuating precautionary cash hoarding tendencies and recalibrating optimal liquidity buffers. Drawing on a two wave, multi source sample of 412 senior finance and operations executives across technology intensive services and advanced manufacturing firms, we employ a two step Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) procedure incorporating Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and latent moderated mediation analysis. The findings indicate that GenAI deployment intensity exerts a significant positive effect on forecasting accuracy (β = 0.487, p < .001), which in turn mediates a significant reduction in excess liquidity buffers. Environmental dynamism significantly moderates the indirect pathway, such that the cash optimizing effect strengthens under heightened uncertainty (index of moderated mediation = 0.142, 95% CI [0.081, 0.210]). The study contributes a micro foundational account of technology enabled financial agility and offers actionable guidance for chief financial officers recalibrating liquidity policy in an algorithmically intermediated environment.

title: Titling under Collective Ownership: How China Decoupled Labor from Land
affiliations: ,  and Northeast Agricultural University

detail.title: Titling under Collective Ownership: How China Decoupled Labor from Land

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a socioeconomic empirical research based on rural household questionnaire surveys. It does not involve human clinical trials, biological experiments, or sensitive personal medical information. The survey was conducted with the verbal consent of all participating farmers.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research. This study was completed independently by the authors without financial support from any funders, institutions or research projects.

detail.abstract: Judged against the market-making benchmark standard in the titling literature, China’s 2013–2018 land certification campaign, the largest property rights formalization in history—appears to underperform, as household land renting-out fails to rise. We argue that evaluating the reform solely through this conventional lens fundamentally misreads the institutional context. Under China’s collective ownership system, certification was implemented alongside the Three-Rights Separation reform, a companion policy that legally unbundled a strictly secured contract right from a transferable operation right. Combining the 2009–2017 National Fixed-Point Survey household panel with a novel certification-timing dataset across 2,008 counties, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences design to estimate the policy’s effects. The data reveal a distinct decoupling signature: Certification reduces defensive land renting-out, a margin the market-making yardstick misinterprets as a failure, while simultaneously freeing rural labor for out-migration and tilting operated land toward consolidation. Although three sharp quantitative hypotheses did not survive falsification, the surviving evidence supports a qualitative institutional reinterpretation. In this context, land titling served as an instrument for managed structural transformation rather than pure market creation.

title: What Static Elicitations Recover When Choices Change Future Opportunities
affiliations: HEC Paris - Operations Management and Information Technology

detail.title: What Static Elicitations Recover When Choices Change Future Opportunities
detail.abstract: Researchers estimate behavioral parameters by inverting static, payoff-only elicitation equations. We show that when the alternatives also change the subject's future opportunities, the recovered coefficient absorbs their value, and derive the exact adjustment: the estimate equals the primitive plus the omitted continuation-value difference, discounted to the divergence date and divided by the equation's sensitivity. One unrestricted elicitation cannot separate them; across arms the coefficients form a linear system determining when the primitive is point identified and how many arms suffice. The continuation problem enters through a sufficient statistic whose content depends on the evaluator: a mean under expected value, a mean and one premium under maxmin or fixed curvature, the full distribution when curvature is unrestricted. We study two applications: a continuation-neutral arm recovers loss aversion, while in monetary timing tasks liquidity values defeat identification of the discount factor; rewards consumed on receipt, with date-stable utility, restore it.

title: The Assistive Exemption: Content Provenance Marking and the Compelled Disclosure of Disability

detail.title: The Assistive Exemption: Content Provenance Marking and the Compelled Disclosure of Disability
detail.abstract: Article 50(2) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act requires providers of generative systems to mark outputs in a machine-readable format so that they are detectable as artificially generated. The obligation carries an express carve-out: it does not apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing. The Commission's July 2026 Guidelines define that exception to cover grammar correction, spellchecking, minor stylistic polishing, machine translation, and, expressly, content that only transforms authentic human input through assistive technologies allowing persons with disabilities to communicate. They also confirm that the exception applies per operation rather than per system. So the drafters did consider disabled users. They considered one kind. The carve-out reaches assistive technology that lets a person communicate without altering semantics; it does not reach assistive technology that helps a person compose or organize, and the same Guidelines place summarization and substantive rewriting back inside the marking duty. The line runs through the middle of the disabled population. The first implementations went further still. In August 2026 Anthropic announced that its models mark generated text worldwide, and its own documentation concedes that a detected mark shows only that text may have been processed by the model, naming proofreading, translation, and summarization as uses it cannot distinguish. Two of those three are inside the Commission's exception. The mark attaches anyway, applies wherever the product is offered rather than to output used in the Union, and reaches personal use the Act excludes from scope. The Code of Practice then decides who reads it. It concedes in operative text that watermark detection for free-form text has lower reliability and may produce misleading or low-confidence results, and it nonetheless guarantees access to a named class of expert users that includes educational and research organisations. It requires that a detection result be downloadable as a digitally signed artifact with a content hash and timestamp. It contains no provision entitling the person whose text was queried to notice, to the receipt, or to any route to contest the result. This Article makes three claims. First, that accessibility enters this regime in one direction only: it constrains how a notice or a detection result is delivered to a reader, never who is marked, and the Guidelines state that Article 50 imposes no distinct accessibility requirements of its own. Second, that the resulting position is a compelled disclosure. The mark says nothing about disability; it says machine involvement, and where an institution restricts that involvement the only defense available to an accommodated author is the accommodation. A facially neutral rule answerable only by disclosing protected status is a disability related inquiry in substance, and existing doctrine already says so. Third, that no doctrine reaches the injury when it occurs. The provider that creates the signal owes the marked person nothing; the institution that acts on it holds a guaranteed right of access and did not create it. Accommodation law is built for a dyad. Provenance marking makes a triad whose third element is a property of the artifact.

title: Local Time against Deployed Code: The Exact Cost Law of Concentrated Liquidity Rebalancing, its Sharp Floor, and its Inversion
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Local Time against Deployed Code: The Exact Cost Law of Concentrated Liquidity Rebalancing, its Sharp Floor, and its Inversion
detail.abstract: Every floor function, trigger line, and threshold in deployed market code is a surface in price space, and automated liquidity management dissipates value where the price meets them. That dissipation obeys one exact law, developed here in three directions and characterised by six theorems. The law is a pathwise identity splitting dissipated value into three terms of a single expansion: a continuous concavity leg, which occupies the slot priced by the loss-versus-rebalancing literature; an event leg, set by the operator’s own geometry; and a monitoring layer. Localised in price, the identity is a measure over the code’s discontinuity set. The event leg is priced exactly. An isolated re-placement pays a mint kerf, the maximum of two log ratios of target share to current share, a potential difference in the position’s composition coordinate computed from the venue’s mint arithmetic rather than assumed. The kerf implies a floor. On a diffusive era every band-maintaining policy in the stated classes dissipates at a rate near twice volatility squared over half-width squared; this tangency constant is sharp in the narrow limit, approached but not attained by two-sided reflection. Corrective swaps replace the constant by the fee scale. The floor is a property of emission, so retention deletes it rather than lowering it. Inverted, the law makes the deployed population a conditional measuring instrument. The naive pooled reading fails, defeated by the operators’ own policy filters; the conditioned small-delay reading identifies integrated jump-tail functionals per pool with explicit error under stated era and monitoring hypotheses, replicating across operator strata within pools. Algebraic, synthetic, production, and bytecode checks support the results: the cost residual at machine precision on 78,908 production rebalances and the exact layer holding against unmodified bytecode on four deployments across three chains. Under the stated landing conditions the jump surcharge closes the loop, hardening the floor at the tails the instrument itself measures.

title: The Evolution of Banking Productivity In Bangladesh (1972–2026): A Non-Parametric Malmquist Productivity Index Analysis of Public, Private, And Co-Operative Intermediaries

detail.title: The Evolution of Banking Productivity In Bangladesh (1972–2026): A Non-Parametric Malmquist Productivity Index Analysis of Public, Private, And Co-Operative Intermediaries
detail.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive, long-term empirical evaluation of financial intermediary productivity in Bangladesh from the post-independence nationalization era of 1972 through the digital transformations and structural consolidations of 2025. Utilizing a non-parametric Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) based Malmquist Productivity Index framework, we decompose Total Factor Productivity (TFP) growth into technical efficiency change (catching-up effect) and technological progress (frontier-shifting effect). We analyze a balanced panel dataset representing State-Owned Commercial Banks (SOCBs), Private Commercial Banks (PCBs), Foreign Commercial Banks (FCBs), and parallel micro-credit/co-operative networks (Somitis). The historical narrative is segmented into four distinct regulatory epochs to track efficiency shifts resulting from key policy shocks, including the 1990 Financial Sector Reform Project (FSRP) and recent asset quality mandates. Our empirical framework models financial capital (deposits) and operating expenditures as primary inputs, while mapping total credits, strategic investments, and non-interest fee income as outputs. The model controls for macroeconomic indicators, asset health (Non-Performing Loan ratios), and parallel informal financial credit density. The findings offer critical structural insights into institutional resource allocation, highlighting policy pathways for optimizing operational productivity amidst a rapidly evolving digital financial ecosystem.

title: Prospects for the Development of The Crypto-Asset Market in Uzbekistan: Challenges and Opportunities
affiliations: Republic of Uzbekistan

detail.title: Prospects for the Development of The Crypto-Asset Market in Uzbekistan: Challenges and Opportunities
detail.abstract: This paper examines the development of the crypto-asset market in the Republic of Uzbekistan between 2018 and 2026 and identifies the constraints and opportunities shaping its trajectory. The study combines documentary analysis of national legal acts, descriptive statistics from open regulatory data, comparative analysis of Central Asian regimes, and SWOT and scenario analysis. Uzbekistan has built a licence-based model of controlled integration in which cryptoasset transactions are lawful but must be executed through domestically licensed providers, with the investment function permitted and the payment function prohibited. Turnover of the licensed segment exceeded USD 2 billion by early 2026 and the country leads Central Asia in the Global Crypto Adoption Index, yet the user base remains below 2% of the population and an extensive unlicensed segment persists. The paper argues that the model has reached the limits of a permission-based approach: further growth is constrained less by weak demand than by the narrow functional scope of permitted operations. The special legal regime for stablecoins and the regulatory sandbox introduced in January 2026 mark a shift from a speculative-investment model towards a payment-infrastructure one. Three scenarios to 2030 and policy recommendations are developed.

title: Stochastic Modeling of Interest Rates and Its Impact on Bond Portfolio Risk
affiliations: and Synthica Research Group

detail.title: Stochastic Modeling of Interest Rates and Its Impact on Bond Portfolio Risk
detail.abstract: Standard fixed-income risk tools discount promised cash flows at a single static rate, an assumption under which a Treasury portfolio held to maturity carries almost no measured risk. We quantify how much risk that convention conceals. An equally weighted two-bond Treasury portfolio, combining a two-year and a ten-year par bond struck on the 17 March 2026 Constant Maturity Treasury curve, is valued under four one-factor short-rate models: drifted Brownian motion, Vasicek, Cox-Ingersoll-Ross, and Hull-White. Each model is simulated by Euler-Maruyama on a monthly grid under a shared seed, and Value at Risk, Expected Shortfall, and loss probability are read from the horizon distribution and compared against a constant-rate point mass. Every simulator is gated against closed-form prices, the risk-neutral drift condition, and exact transition laws before any risk figure is reported. The constant-rate benchmark carries zero dispersion by construction, whereas every stochastic specification produces strictly positive tail risk that widens with bond duration. Mean reversion is the first-order modeling choice: the unrestricted random walk yields a one-year 99% VaR of +16.3% against at most +2.8% for any mean-reverting specification. The Gaussian-versus-positive choice moves the five-year tail by a few percentage points; exact curve fitting moves it by tens of basis points and leaves the width of the loss distribution unchanged. Reported quantiles are risk-neutral comparative statics rather than physical-measure risk forecasts, a distinction we make explicit and quantify.

title: Parents in the Classroom: Strengthening Government Capacity to Deliver Early Childhood Education
affiliations: , World Bank, Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS),  and Royal Holloway, University of London

detail.title: Parents in the Classroom: Strengthening Government Capacity to Deliver Early Childhood Education
detail.abstract: Preschool enrollment has expanded rapidly in low-income countries, but quality has lagged, and evidence on how governments can improve it remains limited. We evaluate Lively Minds, a scalable early childhood program adopted and implemented by Ghana’s Ministry of Education that trains community mothers to deliver structured, play-based activities in public preschools and support children’s learning at home. Using a cluster randomized controlled trial in 80 rural preschools, we find that the program increases cognitive development by 0.12 standard deviations and reduces problem behaviors by 0.10 SD on average. Cognitive gains are similar for children of participating and non-participating mothers, whereas behavioral improvements are concentrated among children of participating mothers. Consistent with this pattern, only participating mothers improve their knowledge of child development and engage in more developmentally supportive interactions with their children at home. These findings suggest that engaging parents — even those with limited formal education — can generate additional benefits beyond those of approaches that rely solely on teachers and paraprofessionals. A cost-benefit analysis indicates that the program’s private benefits substantially exceed its costs, with no adverse effects on mothers’ well-being.

title: Silicon Sampling in Seoul: Conditioning Ablations for LLM Survey Simulation against a Probability Sample
affiliations: ,  and sapiensq

detail.title: Silicon Sampling in Seoul: Conditioning Ablations for LLM Survey Simulation against a Probability Sample
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) conditioned on persona descriptions-"silicon sampling"promise cheap pre-fielding simulation of public-opinion surveys, but validation outside Englishspeaking contexts remains scarce, and the question of how much persona detail to condition on is unresolved. We validate LLM survey simulation against the 2024 Seoul Survey, a probability sample of 5,000 Seoul residents with official weights, across 24 attitudinal and behavioral items. We ablate three conditioning levels: no persona (C0), demographics only (C1), and demographics plus rich synthetic narratives from a census-grounded persona dataset (C2). In frontier commercial models, conditioning buys subgroup ordering at the price of level calibration: demographic conditioning lifts cell-level rank tracking from r ≈ 0 to r = 0.42 while slightly degrading distributional fit, and-contrary to the intuition that richer personas help-synthetic narratives significantly worsen both distributional fit (∆TVD +0.031, 95% CI [+0.029, +0.033]) and subgroup tracking (∆r =-0.067 [-0.113,-0.017]) relative to demographics alone. We propose a hybrid estimator that anchors population levels with the unconditioned model and layers demographic cell deviations on top, attaining the best of both at zero marginal cost. These patterns replicate across two commercial providers but not in two locally-run open-weight models (7.8B and 30B), whose subgroup tracking is a third to an eighth of the commercial models' and in which the narrative penalty is absent or reversed-bounding the results to models capable of tracking subgroups at all. A memorization probe indicates the model cannot recall published aggregates of the target survey, ruling out contamination as the driver. For capable models our results suggest a practical rule: give the model an ID card, not an autobiography-invented biographical detail actively hurts, even when the persona dataset is demographically calibrated.

title: Teaching a Two-Group Comparison with Published Open Data: An R Shiny Application, Its Materials, and Their Verification
affiliations: Nanzan University

detail.title: Teaching a Two-Group Comparison with Published Open Data: An R Shiny Application, Its Materials, and Their Verification

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not required. The study uses only openly published secondary data released under a Creative Commons Attribution licence, and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Statistics courses generally teach statistics as a subject in its own right. What they less often do is show researchers in applied fields how to apply the specific procedures used in their disciplines to the kinds of data they encounter and report the results in a research paper. This short communication reports a set of open teaching materials developed from the perspective of an author whose field is public administration rather than statistics. The materials comprise an R Shiny application that compares a scale score between two independent groups, two slide decks for consecutive 100-minute sessions, and a script that converts a deposited SPSS file and checks the results against those reported in the source article. The application uses Welch's t-test as its default rather than treating it as a fallback, presents a variance check as a description of the data rather than as a rule for selecting the test, places the boxplot before the numerical output, and generates an APA-style reporting sentence in which the interpretation is left blank. Verification used the openly deposited data from a published comparison of nurses in governmental and private hospitals; group means, standard deviations, and test statistics were reproduced to the precision reported. The exercise also revealed two defects in the author's own materials that testing against the bundled example could not have exposed. Reanalysing published open data therefore serves both as a student assignment and as an acceptance test for the materials.

title: Corporate Investment Portfolio with Heterogeneous Time-risk
affiliations: and The University of Osaka

detail.title: Corporate Investment Portfolio with Heterogeneous Time-risk

declarations.funderStatement: This study was supported by the JSPS KAKENHI (grant numbers 22K13434, 24K00272, 24KK0240) and Ishii Memorial Securities Research Promotion Foundation.

detail.abstract: We study a risk-averse firm's optimal portfolio choice among investment projects with heterogeneous time-risk. When projects require an uncertain amount of time before generating revenue, time-risk arises not only at the level of individual projects but also across projects. We show that a firm with a quadratic utility function, despite being risk-averse, inherently seeks time-risk from three distinct perspectives: 1) uncertainty in the order in which projects are completed, 2) uncertainty in the timing of earlier revenue generation within a portfolio, and 3) uncertainty in the timing of revenue generation for each individual project. We also demonstrate that the diversification effect of time-risk always exists, regardless of the distribution of time-risk. Furthermore, we explicitly derive the optimal portfolio and show that, whenever a dominance relationship exists among time-risks, the efficient frontier can be attained by a linear combination of two (possibly hypothetical) projects, regardless of the degree of risk aversion. Lastly, we show that increased uncertainty in the time-dimension improves the efficient frontier, in sharp contrast to the effect of increased uncertainty in the state space from the classical mean-variance framework.

title: Do Large Language Models Reproduce Classic Human Decision Biases?

detail.title: Do Large Language Models Reproduce Classic Human Decision Biases?
detail.abstract: A growing body of work asks whether large language models (LLMs) can stand in for human participants when pretesting survey studies. We evaluate this directly on the heuristics-and-biases battery compiled in Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025), a public dataset built from the answers of more than 2,000 real people. We run 17 classic experiments (framing, the conjunction fallacy, anchoring, sunk cost, and others) through persona-conditioned simulated respondents and score, for each experiment, whether the model produces a statistically significant effect in the direction the original authors reported. Aggregating across an ensemble of instruction-tuned models, counting an effect as reproduced when at least one model in the ensemble shows it, reproduces 15.5 of the 17 effects (91%; the half-point is the endowment effect, which reproduces only partially). For reference, Toubia et al. report that digital twins conditioned on each respondent's own prior answers reproduce the expected effect in 8 of the 16 experiments they tested (50%). The two figures are not a like-for-like contest (the study sets and scoring rules differ), but both point to the same conclusion: the large majority of well-established human effects re-emerge in LLM respondents. We describe where they succeed, where they fail (notably dominator neglect and, partially, the endowment effect), and argue this supports using AI respondents to pretest, not replace, human data collection.

title: Blocking the Giants: Theory and Evidence from the Great Firewall

detail.title: Blocking the Giants: Theory and Evidence from the Great Firewall
detail.abstract: Trade policy increasingly targets individual firms and products rather than entire sectors or countries. This paper develops a framework for evaluating granular trade policies in highly differentiated markets. Using an event-study design, I first show that product-pair elasticities of substitution are systematically related to the similarity between product descriptions. Motivated by this evidence, I develop a general-equilibrium trade model with oligopolistic competition. Products are heterogeneous in their attribute mix and quality, and substitution strength varies continuously with product similarity. I apply the theory to the mobile app sector and evaluate China's Great Firewall Project (GFW). Removing the GFW raises Chinese consumers' utility from app-based leisure but reallocates profits away from Chinese companies (e.g., Tencent) toward foreign companies (e.g., Meta). In the benchmark calibration, this profit shift more than offsets the direct consumer gain: removing the GFW lowers Chinese welfare by 0.146%, while raising welfare by 0.311% in the United States and 0.080% in the rest of the world.

title: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty
affiliations: University of Mannheim and Federal Reserve Board of Governors

detail.title: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty
detail.abstract: How does fiscal policy shape firms' price-setting behavior and aggregate inflation when firms are uncertain about fiscal policy and productivity shocks? We study this question in a general equilibrium model of rationally inattentive price-setting firms, where fiscal policy affects firms’ desired prices through revenue taxes. Public debt changes firms’ incentives to acquire information through two opposing forces: higher debt lowers the stakes of pricing decisions, but makes desired prices more sensitive to tax changes. This trade-off generates a U-shape in firms' attention and inflation volatility with respect to public debt. Using micro data on price setting from euro-area countries, we show that the passthrough of expected cost changes to expected price changes increases in countries' debt-to-GDP ratios, consistent with our model. In general equilibrium, an increase in the debt-to-GDP ratio from 100% to 175% leads to an increase in inflation volatility of about 20% when attention is costly.

title: Nonlinear Shrinkage of Pre-Averaged Realized Covariance Matrices for Minimum-Variance Portfolios

detail.title: Nonlinear Shrinkage of Pre-Averaged Realized Covariance Matrices for Minimum-Variance Portfolios
detail.abstract: Portfolio construction from intraday returns confronts two distortions at once. Microstructure noise and nonsynchronous trading bias the realized covariance matrix; high dimensionality distorts its entire eigenvalue spectrum. The two problems are usually treated in isolation, and the standard fixes work against each other: sampling sparsely to defeat noise throws away the observations that a spectral correction needs, while shrinking the full-frequency realized covariance inherits a spectrum that noise has already corrupted. This paper studies the estimator that addresses both defects jointly, namely nonlinear shrinkage applied to a pre-averaged realized covariance matrix, and characterizes its behavior in the regime where the cross-sectional dimension p grows in step with the noise-robust effective sample size √ n. Because the efficient rate of convergence under noise is n 1/4 , the operative concentration ratio is p/ √ n rather than p/n; the limiting spectral distribution of the pre-averaged matrix is a deformed Marčenko-Pastur law whose shape is governed by the pre-averaging kernel and the noise-to-signal ratio, so the oracle shrinkage function differs from the one implied by treating high-frequency returns as independent draws. I give the oracle shrinkage that minimizes limiting out-of-sample portfolio variance, show that a feasible split-sample estimator attains it, and prove that the resulting global minimum-variance portfolio achieves the oracle out-of-sample variance under joint asymptotics in the cross-section, the span, and the sampling mesh. In simulations calibrated to liquid equity magnitudes, the estimator reduces excess out-of-sample risk over the infeasible oracle by roughly one half relative to linear shrinkage at p = 120, and it is nearly invariant to the level of microstructure noise, whereas shrinkage of the raw realized covariance degrades monotonically as noise rises.

title: Iran as Syntax: Sanctions, Sovereignty, and the AI-mediated Grammar of Threat
affiliations: Universidad de la Republica

detail.title: Iran as Syntax: Sanctions, Sovereignty, and the AI-mediated Grammar of Threat
detail.abstract:
This article introduces sanctioned suffering as a formal problem in AI-mediated
geopolitical discourse. Building on the concepts of responsibility loss and asymmetric
visibility, it examines how generative systems, news summarizers, policy explainers, and
platform-mediated discourse may represent Iran less as a sovereign political society than
as a recurring object of threat, instability, escalation, nuclear risk, proxy activity, and
containment. The paper does not ask whether criticism of the Iranian state is legitimate. It
asks whether AI-generated discourse preserves the grammatical distinction between
criticizing a state, securitizing a society, and obscuring civilian harm produced or
intensified by external pressure.
The central claim is that sanctioned societies can become hyper-visible as geopolitical risks
while remaining weakly visible as affected populations. In discourse about Iran, sanctions,
financial restrictions, overcompliance, diplomatic isolation, and military pressure are often
rendered through neutral administrative or economic language: pressure, restrictions,
compliance, shortages, hardship, inflation, access problems, and supply constraints. Such
formulations may describe harm while weakening the visibility of the actors who impose
or intensify the conditions under which that harm occurs. Threat remains agentive;
suffering becomes indirect, conditional, or unattributed.
Methodologically, the article proposes two measures: the Threat-Conversion Rate and the
Sanctioned Suffering Visibility Index. The first measures the proportion of clauses in
which Iran, Iranian institutions, or Iranian society are represented primarily as sources of
threat rather than as political actors, sovereign entities, or civilian populations affected by
external coercion. The second measures the degree to which civilian harm linked to
sanctions, isolation, financial restrictions, overcompliance, or military pressure remains
grammatically visible as harm with identifiable causes, agents, and affected subjects.
Together, these measures allow AI-mediated geopolitical discourse to be evaluated not
only for bias or misinformation, but for its capacity to preserve or dissolve the grammar of
responsibility.
The paper argues that AI ethics and platform governance require a shift from risk detection
alone toward responsibility detection. A system that can identify dangerous language but
cannot preserve the relation between coercion, civilian harm, and accountable agency
remains structurally incomplete. Sanctioned suffering begins where coercion is renamed
as pressure and civilians disappear into the grammar of risk.

title: Sustainability Challenges in Agriculture: The Case for Millets Revolution (Shree Anna)
affiliations: Indian Institute of Foreign Trade - Centre for WTO Studies and Indian Institute of Foreign Trade - Centre for WTO Studies

detail.title: Sustainability Challenges in Agriculture: The Case for Millets Revolution (Shree Anna)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: none
declarations.funderStatement: no

detail.abstract:
India placed millets on the global stage: the National Year of Millets in 2018 and the UN International Year of Millets in 2023, on the argument that awareness and demand creation would revive a crop that once made up roughly 40 per cent of India's cultivated grain and now accounts for about 20 per cent. This paper tests that proposition against the production, cost, procurement and trade record, and finds no revival. Area under Shree Anna fell from 350.6 lakh hectares in the 1970s to 128.7 lakh hectares in the 2020s; yields more than doubled over the same period, yet production has been essentially flat. Returns over cost C2 are negative for jowar, ragi and bajra in most major producing states across most of the period, barley being the exception because it is grown largely for industrial use. Procurement of Nutri-cereals did not rise even in the International Year of Millets, and procurement as a share of marketed surplus fell from 7.2 to 5.6 per cent. Coarse cereals account for 3.8 per cent of rural and 2.4 per cent of urban cereal consumption. The binding constraint, therefore, lies in profitability, processing capacity, and assured offtake, not in awareness. 

The paper further shows that price support and exports operate on separate axes: procured grain is confined to decentralised procurement and welfare distribution within the procuring State, while exports are sourced entirely from open markets, remain under one per cent of rice export value, and move as raw grain at unit values below those realised on rice. On market access, it corrects a common assumption. Millets are named individually in Codex Group 020, in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 and in the 2022 expansion of US Crop Group 15-22; what is scarce is not classification but millet-specific residue data, so that the European default of 0.01 mg/kg and the United States zero-tolerance rule operate as a de facto barrier, with mycotoxins the more binding practical constraint. The effective regime confronting millets is thus stricter, not laxer, than that facing rice and wheat. India's negotiating ask should accordingly be technical rather than declaratory: JMPR sponsorship, residue trials through ICAR-IIMR, and Codex MRLs for small millets, alongside remunerative procurement, credit, and post-harvest investment at home.

title: The Aspirational Scale Effect: A Theory of How Larger Goals Can Raise the Probability of Reaching Lower Thresholds

detail.title: The Aspirational Scale Effect: A Theory of How Larger Goals Can Raise the Probability of Reaching Lower Thresholds
detail.abstract: This paper develops the Aspirational Scale Effect (ASE): the proposition that choosing a goal substantially above a desired minimum outcome can, under defined conditions, increase the probability of attaining that lower outcome. Consider three students beginning with equivalent money, education, time, ability, information, and social support. The first aims to become a millionaire, the second a billionaire, and the third a trillionaire. The millionaire goal may organize behavior around a million-dollar pathway. The billionaire goal may force the design of scalable companies, technology, ownership, capital networks, and global distribution; even if the student never becomes a billionaire, those choices may increase the probability of becoming a millionaire. The trillionaire goal may expand the design space further and may make millionaire status comparatively more attainable, while billionaire status remains less probable and trillionaire status extraordinarily improbable. The theory does not claim that thought, visualization, or manifestation alone changes reality. Rather, an internal aspiration can alter attention, effort, persistence, resource mobilization, strategy search, identity, risk perception, and the scale of systems a person attempts to build. These mechanisms can shift the distribution of possible outcomes. The paper integrates goal-setting theory, self-efficacy, implementation intentions, reference-point effects, and research on stretch goals. It proposes a nonlinear mathematical model in which performance initially rises with aspirational scale, then plateaus or declines when the goal becomes non-credible, cognitively overwhelming, under-resourced, or ethically distorting. The result is a conditional inverted-U: thinking bigger can raise the probability of reaching a smaller threshold, but only until the aspirational target exceeds the actor's zone of productive credibility. Six testable hypotheses and a preregistered field experiment are proposed. The practical conclusion is a dual-target architecture: hold a large directional ambition, define a credible operating target, convert it into proximal process goals, preserve learning and ethical guardrails, and measure whether the larger target actually changes behavior.

title: Objective-Oriented Quantitative Investment: A Specification-Driven Framework for Automated Synthesis of Trading Strategy Pipelines
affiliations: Huatai Securities

detail.title: Objective-Oriented Quantitative Investment: A Specification-Driven Framework for Automated Synthesis of Trading Strategy Pipelines
detail.abstract: Automated quantitative research has made striking progress-AutoML pipeline synthesis, neural architecture search, reinforcement-learned alpha mining, and LLM-agent research loops all promise to automate the construction of trading strategies. Yet every one of these systems answers the same question: which strategy scores highest on a scalar metric? We argue this question is incomplete. Professional investors do not order "the highest return"; they order an identity-pure stock-selection alpha uncontaminated by style exposure, resilient in unilateral market declines, within turnover and capacity budgets. We call the incumbent paradigm result-oriented and propose, in its place, Objective-Oriented Quantitative Investment (OOQI): a specification-driven framework in which (i) the full strategy pipeline is modeled as a typed design space of interchangeable modules with explicit interface contracts (8.85 × 10 8 assemblies in our reference instantiation, high 10 8 s after legality pruning); (ii) investor intent is formalized as a strategy profile specification-a composable language of measurable, falsifiable clauses drawn from eight requirement families, with hard/soft semantics, priorities, and an interaction algebra capturing synergy and conflict among objectives; and (iii) a compiler translates specifications into constrained assemblies, verifies satisfaction clause-by-clause, and iterates with attribution. Because search over large assembly spaces inflates apparent satisfaction, we develop a verification protocol that treats the satisfaction rate itself as a statistical object subject to deflation for search width, isolated temporal holdout, and random-assembly null models. An illustrative synthetic demonstration with 32 pipeline assemblies shows that result-oriented selection attains the top in-sample information ratio while satisfying only 25% of the specification, whereas specification-driven selection satisfies 100% of it at a measurable 5.5% score cost-the two paradigms provably select different strategies. OOQI reframes automated quantitative research from optimization of a number to satisfaction of an identity, and supplies the formal apparatus-language, compiler, and statistics-to make that reframing rigorous. A theory of optimal assembly accompanies the framework: satisfaction-driven synthesis is NP-hard in general yet constant-factor approximable in a conflict-free (submodular) regime; specifications form a lattice dual to assemblies, yielding identity inference and zero-cost clause completion; each clause carries a Lagrangian shadow price-a clause-level transfer coefficient; and rolling re-certification can be made anytime-valid via e-processes, turning alpha decay into certificate expiry.

title: The Post-Bretton Woods Transition: A New Multipolar World with Four

detail.title: The Post-Bretton Woods Transition: A New Multipolar World with Four
detail.abstract: Reserve currency transitions are not orderly handoffs between sovereign states. This paper argues they are contested outcomes among four structurally distinct formations (Sovereign States, the Financial Industrial Complex (FIC), the Military Industrial Complex (MIC), and the Technology Industrial Complex (TIC)) whose interests diverge even when their short-term strategies align. The Quadruple Power Architecture (QPA) is the analytical framework developed here to map those divergences and their distributional consequences. The empirical anchor is straightforward: the U.S. dollar's share of global official reserves has fallen from approximately 72 percent in 2001 to 56.92 percent in Q3 2025, though much of the 2 recent decline reflects exchange-rate valuation effects rather than active portfolio rebalancing (IMF COFER 2025), while central bank gold purchases have exceeded 1,000 metric tons in each of the past three years, the highest accumulation rate since the 1950s (World Gold Council 2025). The central distributional argument is that the FIC occupies the structural first-access position in any monetary expansion: closest to the point of money creation through primary dealer relationships, and closest to the governance of productive assets through proxy voting authority. The data are consistent with this positional advantage producing distributional concentration, though the causal identification remains incomplete. Supporting evidence on critical mineral supply chains, equity ownership concentration, and defense procurement is developed in the body.

title: Don't Know is the New Literacy: Financial Knowledge When Delegation Became Free
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Don't Know is the New Literacy: Financial Knowledge When Delegation Became Free
detail.abstract: Between 2009 and 2024 the price of delegating financial decisions fell toward zero: equity fund expense ratios dropped from 0.82 to 0.40 percent while automatic enrollment spread. Americans' Big Three scores fell 14 percent, "don't know" (DK) answers rose 30 percent, and financial behavior improved. DK answers did not become noise: their predictive content doubled and now exceeds that of correct answers. Using six waves of the National Financial Capability Study, I show the DK margin is consistent with delegation displacing knowledge, and that flipping the Big Three scoring rule doubles its predictive power.

title: Drowning in Debt: How Climate Shocks and Digital Relief Lags Trigger Post-Flood Vulnerability Cycles in Sivasagar, Assam
affiliations: Dibrugarh University

detail.title: Drowning in Debt: How Climate Shocks and Digital Relief Lags Trigger Post-Flood Vulnerability Cycles in Sivasagar, Assam
detail.abstract: This study evaluates the socioeconomic impacts of floods on 400 households in the Sivasagar district of Assam [ASDMA]. Using an easy-to-understand Livelihood Vulnerability Index, we analyze how physical flood exposure, informal jobs, and government relief delays influence family debt. The district shows a high vulnerability score, with Sivasagar Circle and Nazira facing the highest risks. Our findings reveal two clear trends: first, longer flood immersion and informal jobs are the primary drivers of household vulnerability. Second, there is a direct link between flood damage and debt traps. For every ₹10,000 in asset damage, a household takes on an average of ₹3,479 in new debt, while each day of delay in receiving government relief drives an extra ₹442 in local borrowing. To break this cycle, we recommend introducing automated insurance payouts, expanding non-farm job training, and building stronger river embankments.

title: Answering FINRA's Question: Why US Financial Literacy Fell and What it now Measures, 2009-2024
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Answering FINRA's Question: Why US Financial Literacy Fell and What it now Measures, 2009-2024
detail.abstract: The National Financial Capability Study, fielded by FINRA, asks why Americans' Big Three financial literacy scores fell 0.40 items (0.35 SD), 2009-2021, while their behavior improved. People learn what they think is worth knowing. The decline is deepest among workers without employer plans (0.51 versus 0.35 items for the covered), while emergency saving rose 19 points: knowledge investment, not disengagement. Knowledge responds to perceived return (the inflation shock raised the item 5.3 points), institutions carry behavior (auto-IRAs raised planning 8.2 points), and covering the excluded restored knowledge in 2024. The fall is predominantly a withdrawal of demand, not lost ability.

title: Who Can Compel Whom: Institutional Design For Buyer Power in Concentrated Supply Chains: A Comparison of Six Regimes
affiliations: Lincoln Regulatory Consulting

detail.title: Who Can Compel Whom: Institutional Design For Buyer Power in Concentrated Supply Chains: A Comparison of Six Regimes
detail.abstract: Australia and the United Kingdom have both legislated against the same structural problem: concentrated buyers dictating terms to a fragmented supply base, in markets where the ordinary law of contract assumes a bargain the parties were free to strike. They have built strikingly different institutions to address it. This paper compares six — the United Kingdom’s Groceries Code Adjudicator; Australia’s abolished Road Safety Remuneration Tribunal; and the four regimes that now constitute Australia’s general machinery: the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission administering the mandatory Food and Grocery Code, the National Heavy Vehicle Regulator administering Chain of Responsibility duties, the New South Wales contract determination system, and Victoria’s owner-driver regime — against nine dimensions drawn from the primary instruments. Three findings emerge, and none of them is the one the comparative literature would predict. First, the decisive design variable is the trigger. Whether the weaker party can compel the stronger to submit to a determination, without the stronger party’s consent, divides these six regimes more sharply than the weight of their sanctions, the breadth of their jurisdiction, or the resources of the body administering them. Three of the six give the weaker party that power; two withhold it, one of them by express drafting while appearing to confer it; and the sixth, the abolished Tribunal, held a dispute jurisdiction it barely used. Second, enforcement output runs inverse to enforcement power. The two regimes with the heaviest penalties available — the Food and Grocery Code, at up to the greater of $10 million, three times the benefit, or 10 per cent of adjusted turnover; and the Groceries Code Adjudicator, at 1 per cent of United Kingdom turnover — have between them produced, in sixteen months and thirteen years respectively, no penalty at all. The regime with the smallest penalties on the table, Victoria’s, at $5,227.50 for a body corporate, is the one whose determination pathway is used. Third, the difference in provenance between the two dedicated bodies is real and is not the same claim as a causal account of survival. The Adjudicator exists because a competition authority made a statutory finding of an adverse effect on competition and issued a remedial order. The Tribunal existed because its Act asserted a proposition its own commissioned analyses could not substantiate. That is a difference in the epistemic footing of the two institutions, verifiable from the instruments, and it bears on what each could defend. Whether it explains why one survived and the other did not is a question this paper expressly does not answer, because the base rate of institutional destruction among Australian federal industrial bodies has not been established and the comparison is uncontrolled. The paper closes with what a designer working within Australian constitutional constraints can and cannot build, and identifies the design features already enacted somewhere in these six regimes that no Australian instrument currently combines.

title: A Right to Delegate to AI: The Regulatory Safety Halo and the Acceleration of Agentic Consumer Markets

detail.title: A Right to Delegate to AI: The Regulatory Safety Halo and the Acceleration of Agentic Consumer Markets
detail.abstract: The European Law Institute's Guiding Principles and Model Rules on Digital Assistants for Consumer Contracts (DACC) propose a consumer right to use a digital assistant in business-to-consumer contractual relations. The DACC's broad definition encompasses consumer AI agents: applications that interpret consumer objectives and exercise discretion over transactional actions. The right would recognise agent use as a protected form of market participation, rather than merely preserve consumer protection when an assistant is used. This article examines two concerns. First, legal recognition and accompanying safeguards may create a regulatory safety halo, leading consumers to overestimate agents' technical reliability and the effectiveness of remedies for unwanted outcomes. Second, recognition may accelerate agentic consumer markets, disproportionately benefiting incumbents in adjacent digital markets and promoting concentration and private rulemaking, to which the DMA and EU competition law provide only partial responses. The article argues that legislation should determine the essential rules governing delegation and market contestability before recognising a general right to use a digital assistant encompassing consumer agents. Technical implementation should promote interoperability and contestability, constrain the normative choices left to standardisation bodies, and mitigate the legitimacy deficiencies of the existing European standardisation process.

title: Disclosed Futures Exposure and Asynchronous Closing Valuation: Evidence from Korean Daily-Reset ETFs
affiliations: Hanyang University, Chung-Ang University and Hanyang University

detail.title: Disclosed Futures Exposure and Asynchronous Closing Valuation: Evidence from Korean Daily-Reset ETFs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
