title: Book review of Rewiring Democracy: How AI Will Transform Our Politics, Government, and Citizenship, by Bruce Schneier and Nathan E. Sanders
affiliations: Thompson Rivers University - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Book review of Rewiring Democracy: How AI Will Transform Our Politics, Government, and Citizenship, by Bruce Schneier and Nathan E. Sanders

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Law and Information Technology, volume 34, 2026[10.1093/ijlit/eaag011]

detail.abstract: This book makes an incisive and technically informed contribution to a rapidly growing body of work on AI and politics. Its central chapters survey the tangible ways AI will alter democratic practices, including political campaigning, lawmaking, administration, and legal judgment. The book is framed by the authors’ conception of democracy as “an information system that translates individual preferences into group policy decisions”, a system that can be optimized through effective use of AI. This conception has its merits, but it underplays democracy as a normative order structured by constitutional limits, institutional friction, public reasoning, and commitments to political equality — and leads the authors, in places, to understate AI’s potential impact on some of its most important dimensions.

title: Sharing the Spotlight? Credit Attribution, Assortative Collaboration, and Creator Stratification on Content Platforms
affiliations: , Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information & Systems Management and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: Sharing the Spotlight? Credit Attribution, Assortative Collaboration, and Creator Stratification on Content Platforms
detail.abstract: Collaboration is central to the creator economy, yet opaque credit attribution makes joint production risky when contributors cannot verify or monetize their individual roles. Major platforms have introduced formal credit systems to make collaboration visible, but evidence remains limited on whether these systems increase collaboration, how they change partner selection, and which creators benefit. We examine these questions on Bilibili, a major video-sharing platform that piloted a formal credit attribution system for music creators. We develop a conceptual model in which creators trade off cross-audience exposure against collaboration costs and then test its predictions using a Difference-inDifferences design augmented by Two-Stage Least Squares estimation. We find that the credit system increases collaboration overall, but the increase is concentrated among more popular creators, who primarily form partnerships with status peers and thereby strengthen assortative matching. The effect is insignificant in domains where sole authorship and creative authenticity carry high reputational value. Downstream performance analyses reveal an incentive-benefit mismatch. Less popular creators receive the largest relative performance gains from credited collaboration but adopt the system at the lowest rates, and their gains dissipate more quickly after the trial. The study identifies reputational infrastructure as a governance primitive distinct from coordination infrastructure in IT-enabled collaboration. It also shows that formal credit changes the tradeoff between cross-audience exposure and credit dilution in mass-audience content markets. Finally, it demonstrates that a neutral and voluntary attribution system can unintentionally amplify the Matthew Effect when formal credit interacts with status homophily. These findings offer implications for platforms that seek to encourage collaboration without deepening creator stratification.

title: The Economic Consequences of Attacks on Wildberries Warehouses: Impact on the E-Commerce Market, Logistics and the Ecosystem of Sellers

detail.title: The Economic Consequences of Attacks on Wildberries Warehouses: Impact on the E-Commerce Market, Logistics and the Ecosystem of Sellers
detail.abstract: The article examines the economic consequences of the attacks by unmanned aerial vehicles on the warehouse complexes of the Wildberries marketplace in Elektrostal and Kotovsk on 18 July 2026, as well as the earlier fire at the warehouse in Shushary in January 2024. On the basis of the analysis of expert estimates of direct losses, of the loss of storage capacity, of the redistribution of the logistical load and of contractual mechanisms of the distribution of risks, the systemic impact on the marketplace, on sellers, on the insurance market and on the segment of warehouse real estate is identified. It is shown that the principal economic burden falls on sellers, while the marketplace, by means of amendments to the offer and of insurance instruments, is minimizing its own losses.

title: Leadership Characteristic and Loyalty
affiliations: Politeknik Ungku Omar, Politeknik Tuanku Sultanah Bahiyah and Seberang Perai Polytechnic, Penang, Malaysia

detail.title: Leadership Characteristic and Loyalty
detail.abstract: Performance is a priority for the organization to keep remaining in the market. Leadership characteristics are required to build up and increase loyalty among the employees. Throughout, good characteristics, for instance listening skills, empathy, and ability to motivate, may cause employees to be happy and satisfaction to lead loyalty. In addition, loyalty can contribute to better employee performance where they utilize skills, experience, and knowledge to achieve objectives. This study discusses how good leadership characteristics can enhance loyalty and vice versa. Performance is also related to leadership characteristics, where an employee is willing to work for the organization if they have a good relationship with the leader.

title: Racial Bias in Team Selection: Experimental Evidence from a Fictional Soccer Lineup
affiliations: and University of Bayreuth - Faculty of Law, Business and Economics

detail.title: Racial Bias in Team Selection: Experimental Evidence from a Fictional Soccer Lineup
detail.abstract: We propose a controlled and incentive-compatible design to study racial bias in team-selection decisions. In an online experiment, participants select a soccer lineup from fictitious players whose objective quality is described by numerical attributes. For each player profile, we randomly assign an AI-generated portrait depicting either a Black or a White player, allowing us to isolate the effect of racial appearance. Overall, we find no systematic evidence that White player versions are selected more frequently than otherwise identical Black versions. We also compare generic-team and national-team framing, but find no systematic amplification of racial bias.

title: Emergency Arbitration and Interim Measures in International Commercial Arbitration: A Comparative Analysis of the ICC 2026 and SIAC 2025 Rules
affiliations: Senior Judicial Magistrate at Bangladesh Judicial Service

detail.title: Emergency Arbitration and Interim Measures in International Commercial Arbitration: A Comparative Analysis of the ICC 2026 and SIAC 2025 Rules
detail.abstract: Emergency arbitration has become a central component of modern institutional arbitration because the period before constitution of the arbitral tribunal is often the moment at which commercial rights are most vulnerable. Assets may be dissipated, evidence may be destroyed, contractual performance may be disrupted, confidential information may be misused, or a transaction may be irreversibly altered before a tribunal is able to act. The 2026 ICC Arbitration Rules and the 2025 SIAC Rules respond to this problem through sophisticated but materially different architectures for emergency and interim relief. This article offers a comparative doctrinal analysis of those regimes. It argues that the ICC 2026 framework is principally access-expansive and jurisdictionally flexible: it expressly accommodates emergency applications against certain non-signatories and introduces preliminary orders that may, where necessary, be issued without prior notice. The SIAC 2025 framework is more procedurally engineered: it permits pre-notice applications, targets appointment of an emergency arbitrator within 24 hours, authorises an order or award within 14 days, and contains a detailed protective preliminary order procedure with rapid disclosure and expiry safeguards. Both systems preserve recourse to national courts and the subsequent authority of the constituted tribunal. Their central difference therefore lies not in whether urgent relief exists, but in how each institution balances speed, notice, jurisdictional reach, enforceability, and procedural legitimacy. The article concludes that SIAC offers greater ex ante procedural certainty, while the ICC offers greater flexibility in complex multi-party disputes; in both regimes, however, the effectiveness of emergency relief ultimately depends upon careful coordination between institutional rules, the law of the seat, and the enforcement forum.

title: Sorted Out: Effective Access, Lender Sorting, and Racial Disparities in PPP Loan Forgiveness
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Sorted Out: Effective Access, Lender Sorting, and Racial Disparities in PPP Loan Forgiveness
detail.abstract: Roughly 72 percent of Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) borrowers with personal-name loan records left the race field blank. Any disparity analysis restricted to self-reported race is therefore silent about most of this borrower segment. Using a race-inference model trained solely on Florida, Georgia, and North Carolina voter-registration records, we measure loan forgiveness outcomes for 4,732,593 personal-name loan records (approximately 4,048,007 unique borrowers), 90.8 percent of all individual-owner PPP loan records. Among borrowers who did not report race, those classified as Black were 12.92 percentage points less likely to receive forgiveness than those classified as White, conditional on state, two-digit industry, program draw round, and firm size (n=4,732,585, two-way ZCTA×lender clustered SE 1.48), with an empirically defensible range of approximately 11.3–12.9 points. The gap rises monotonically with classifier accuracy on a fixed common sample, consistent with attenuation from proxy misclassification rather than geographic circularity; calibration on disclosed-race borrowers implies a gap of 14.95–15.31 points among non-disclosers. Adding fixed effects for 4,600 originating lenders reduces the gap to 4.87 percentage points, implying that roughly 62.3 percent of the aggregate disparity is absorbed by lender fixed effects. We report this as an accounting decomposition; it does not identify the causal effect of lender choice or within-lender treatment. An estimated 61.5 percent of the between-lender component runs through a single margin: 34 nationwide online platform lenders forgave at rates roughly 15.60 points lower, and 91.4 percent of predicted-Black borrowers' loans came through that channel against 37.7 percent of predicted-White borrowers'. Black borrowers are also concentrated in tracts with systematically fewer bank branches — patterns consistent with, but not establishing causation for, geographic banking access as a mechanism, and specific to tract rather than ZIP code scale. Despite this sorting, physical community-bank proximity is similar across minority-share quintiles; the difference is borrower volume per nearby branch — roughly 3.2 times higher in the highest-minority tracts — suggesting effective access depends on relationship formation and institutional throughput rather than physical presence alone.

title: Economic Development in the Shadow of War
affiliations: and

detail.title: Economic Development in the Shadow of War
detail.abstract: This paper provides causal evidence that the mere risk of war — absent actual conflict — imposes substantial economic costs. Our setting exploits NATO's Cold War defense line against a potential Soviet invasion, which created a geographic discontinuity in war risk within West Germany. A leak of classified defense plans in 1977 made this discontinuity salient to the public. We show that war risk distorted firm behavior on the exposed side of the defense line: firm entry declined, and incumbent firms reduced investment. These responses caused persistent regional divergence. Decades after the Cold War ended, incomes remain significantly lower in areas once exposed to higher war risk.

title: Algorithmic Threshold Optimization: Quantitative Modeling of Multiplier Distributions in Crash Games
affiliations: Indian Statistical Institute

detail.title: Algorithmic Threshold Optimization: Quantitative Modeling of Multiplier Distributions in Crash Games
detail.abstract: Crash is a widely played casino game that blends strategic decision-making, probability, and computational analysis, particularly from the perspective of the house. This paper presents an optimization algorithm aimed at minimizing the casino's guaranteed positive earnings while simultaneously maximizing the number of players who win some amount during a given round. Since Crash is inherently a multiplayer game, players place random investment amounts at different points in time, which makes it difficult for any individual player to judge, before the round even begins, whether their intended investment is comparatively high or low, and consequently, how much risk they are actually taking on. The core objective of the proposed algorithm is to determine an optimal stopping multiplier that balances both the casino's and the players' interests. Notably, the algorithm remains unaffected by changes in the number of players or by variation in investment amounts, although in practice casinos typically impose a fixed range on permissible investments. Beyond this, the algorithm can help professional players make more informed decisions about how much to invest and how much risk they are comfortable accepting. We further analyze the algorithm's computational complexity and its stopping-multiplier statistics to give a fuller picture of how it behaves in practice.

title: A Model-Agnostic Level-Set Approach for Prescriptive Analytics
affiliations: Julius-Maximilians-University Wuerzburg, Business Administration & Economics and Business Administration & Economics

detail.title: A Model-Agnostic Level-Set Approach for Prescriptive Analytics
detail.abstract: Data-driven approaches that leverage machine learning for stochastic optimization with contextual information (`prescriptive analytics’) have received considerable attention in recent years. However, existing approaches often rely on the inherent properties of specific models or require problem-specific modifications and training. Motivated by this limitation, we propose a novel framework that allows practitioners to leverage any machine learning model for prescriptive analytics. We introduce a new class of kernel functions that measure similarity through proximity in the prediction space (`level-set approach’). The resulting kernel values can be integrated into existing data-driven optimization techniques that rely on sample weighting or kernel-based transformations. We establish asymptotic optimality under mild assumptions when our method is applied to weighted sample average approximation and demonstrate consistent translation of predictive into prescriptive performance through various numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world data. Our experiments show that using state-of-the-art models within our framework yields substantial cost reductions relative to existing benchmarks.

title: Impact of ESG Ratings on the Performance of S&P 100 Firms

detail.title: Impact of ESG Ratings on the Performance of S&P 100 Firms
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between ESG ratings and the financial performance of S&P 100 firms from 2021 to 2025. This study uses pooled OLS regression on Bloomberg Terminal data, regressing Return on Equity against ESG Score, Net Debt/Equity, and Tobin's Q across 447 firm-year observations from 100 of the United States largest publicly listed companies. ESG Score is positively linked to ROE but not statistically significant (β = 3.740, p = 0.268). Net Debt/Equity (β = 28.899, p < 0.001) and Tobin's Q (β = 4.166, p < 0.001) are both significant. The regression model explains 41.7% of the variance in ROE (R² = 0.4174, F = 105.82). Bloomberg's ESG rating measures how broadly a firm reports on ESG topics, not how it performs on them. No measurable improvement in ROE is found from higher Bloomberg ESG scores in the S&P 100 over this period. Existing literature in this area predominantly uses the S&P 500, Refinitiv or MSCI scores, and data ending before 2021. This paper differs from prior literature in that it uses the S&P 100, Bloomberg's composite, the 2021-2025 period, and ROE rather than ROA.

title: The Self-Preservation Psychodynamics of Leadership: An Integrated Model of Expectations, Follower Response, and Leader Influence
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Self-Preservation Psychodynamics of Leadership: An Integrated Model of Expectations, Follower Response, and Leader Influence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Berkley Institute of Leadership (Pty) Limited

detail.abstract: Leadership research has converged on a broadly relational definition of the phenomenon: leadership is influence exercised in the service of shared goals. What remains under-theorised is why influence succeeds with some followers and in some moments, and fails, or curdles into resistance and sabotage, in others. This paper presents the Self-Preservation Psychodynamics of Leadership (SPPL) model in its integrated, mature form, built across two tiers that stand in a strict hierarchy rather than as parallel or interchangeable accounts. Tier 1 states a claim about human beings as such: we are driven by the Self-Preservation Drive (SPD), an evolved imperative to protect physical and psychological safety, identity coherence, belonging, and agency, expressed through a single governing valence, movement toward Gain and away from Loss, and organised beneath conscious awareness by specific psychodynamic structures, including unconscious motivation, attachment-based dependency, transference, defence, shadow and archetype, and ego state. Tier 2 states a claim about leadership specifically: we are influenced via the SPD. Because human beings are driven by the SPD, leadership, understood as the exercise of influence, can only ever operate by engaging that same drive, well or badly, deliberately or not. Tier 2 supplies the leader's practical operating model, an applied framework built around an expectation continuum, running from a current state (EXP) to a desired End Game, and unfolding across four interconnected Expectation Domains, Psyche (the individual), Logic (the mechanics of goal pursuit), Tribe (the collective), and Ethos (shared principles, values, and moral framework), through which the SPD and its psychodynamic structures are actually engaged, managed, and directed in real organisational settings. The model is grounded in, and draws together without significant prior integration, classical and contemporary psychodynamic theory, affective and threat neuroscience, attachment theory, terror management theory, social identity theory, prospect theory and regulatory focus theory, self-determination theory, goal-setting theory, general systems theory, and complexity leadership theory. Fourteen testable propositions are derived and organised by domain. The paper closes with the model's scope conditions, standing critiques, practical implications, and a doctoral research agenda through which its propositions can be empirically examined. The Tier 2 operating model developed here is intended to function as a practical blueprint in its own right: a working guide deliberately structured to be graspable at a practitioner's level despite the psychological complexity it condenses, and built with a specific further application in view, namely as the conceptual foundation for AI-agent tooling capable of supporting and reinforcing psychodynamically informed leadership practice in real time.

title: Climate Policy for Coordination
affiliations: Utrecht University and Department of Economics, University of Gothenburg

detail.title: Climate Policy for Coordination
detail.abstract: Decarbonizing basic materials industries requires coordinated investment between downstream firms adopting abatement technologies and upstream input providers. We model the resulting indirect network effects, which generate a no-investment equilibrium alongside a coordinated one. Carbon pricing and non-discriminatory subsidies cannot resolve this coordination failure without overshooting the optimum. Subsidies targeted at firms below a cost threshold implement the optimal coordinated equilibrium without distortion. We further show that excluding the lowest-cost firms, who invest voluntarily once others lead, shrinks the subsidized group, and that targeting remains effective under imperfect observability and imprecise targeting. Our results provide formal support for targeted industrial policy.

title: Recursive Contraction and Economic State Stability: A Mathematical Framework for Residual-Based Policy Dynamics
affiliations: Universal Standard Axiom Corp

detail.title: Recursive Contraction and Economic State Stability: A Mathematical Framework for Residual-Based Policy Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper develops a recursive mathematical framework for analyzing stability in an economic state system through a three-stage operator consisting of reasoning, reflection, and refinement. The central construction is deliberately separated from any direct projection onto a desired equilibrium set. Instead, the policy process operates on an economic residual vector measuring deviations from specified target conditions. The resulting recursive system is represented as S_{k+1}=(R_{refine}\circ R_{reflect}\circ R_{reason})(S_{k}). The paper establishes sufficient conditions under which the induced residual dynamics constitute a contraction mapping. In the exactly linear case, the residual process reduces to e_{k+1}=Me_{k} and asymptotic convergence follows from the spectral-radius condition \rho(M) < 1. For the nonlinear case, a global contraction condition on the residual transition operator yields a unique fixed point by the Banach fixed-point theorem. When the zero-residual state is itself a fixed point, uniqueness implies convergence of every admissible residual trajectory to that state. Inflation is treated as one component of the residual rather than as a constraint imposed through projection. Consequently, convergence of the inflation component follows from the stability of the complete residual system. The framework therefore converts a normative economic objective into a falsifiable dynamical-systems hypothesis. The key empirical and computational question is not whether a model can be constructed to return zero inflation, but whether economically defensible transition relationships generate a contraction on the relevant state domain.

title: Government Procurement Efficiency and Its Determinants: The Mediating Roles of Process Quality and Procedural Innovation in Indonesian Local Government
affiliations: Sam Ratulangi University, Universiy of Sam Ratulangi, Sam Ratulangi University and

detail.title: Government Procurement Efficiency and Its Determinants: The Mediating Roles of Process Quality and Procedural Innovation in Indonesian Local Government
detail.abstract: Government procurement efficiency has become an important issue in public sector governance, particularly in the context of digital procurement transformation and increasing administrative complexity. This study aims to analyze the effects of technical competency, managerial competency, process quality, and procedural innovation on government procurement efficiency within the Provincial Government of North Sulawesi, Indonesia. The study also examines the mediating roles of process quality and procedural innovation in the relationships between procurement competencies and procurement efficiency. This study employed a quantitative approach using Structural Equation Modeling-Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). Data were collected through structured questionnaires distributed to 157 Commitment Making Officials (Pejabat Pembuat Komitmen/PPK) involved in government procurement activities within regional government institutions. The analysis was conducted using SmartPLS 4.0 to evaluate both direct and indirect relationships among the research variables. The findings indicate that managerial competency and procedural innovation had positive and significant effects on government procurement efficiency, while technical competency and process quality did not demonstrate significant direct effects. Furthermore, procedural innovation significantly mediated the relationships between technical competency and procurement efficiency, as well as between managerial competency and procurement efficiency. In contrast, process quality did not demonstrate a significant mediating role. The study highlights the strategic importance of managerial capability and procedural innovation in improving procurement efficiency within digital governance environments. The findings contribute to the development of public procurement literature by integrating Human Capital Theory, Resource-Based View (RBV), and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) in the context of government procurement governance. Practically, the study suggests that government institutions should strengthen procedural innovation, digital procurement implementation, and managerial capability to improve procurement performance and organizational responsiveness.

title: Optimal Pricing and Hedging of SOFR Derivatives
affiliations: King's College London and King's College London

detail.title: Optimal Pricing and Hedging of SOFR Derivatives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: This research was partially funded by EPSRC Grant Number EP/T517963/1.

detail.abstract: Thousands of SOFR derivatives are available in exchanges and OTC, but the market remains illiquid and incomplete. Such a market is beyond the scope of classic risk-neutral approaches that imply linear pricing rules and, at best, approximate hedging strategies whose hedging error may be difficult to quantify. This paper develops an indifference pricing model which is consistent with observed derivative quotes, the agent's financial position and views about the uncertain future as well as risk preferences as described by a convex risk measure. In addition to prices and hedging strategies, the model gives an explicit description of the hedging error and the associated risk. The approach is illustrated numerically using hundreds of CME-listed derivatives to price and hedge unreplicable OTC SOFR derivatives. The indifference prices are computed in less than a minute on a regular PC. We find that the optimal hedging portfolios tend to be sparse but still provide good approximations of the derivative payouts.

title: The Price of Error Reversibility as a Factor of Production

detail.title: The Price of Error Reversibility as a Factor of Production

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no funding for this article

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces reversibility as a factor of production purchased ex ante.

Reversibility, denoted ρ, is the capacity of an institutional environment to allow an agent to return to a viable state after an error, at a finite and known cost; by reducing the effective loss from failure, it governs an economy's volume of experimentation and operates as a factor of production in its own right. 

An agent installs capital and chooses, at a cost, the degree 𝜌∈[0,1] to which the stake can be undone once uncertainty resolves. Five results follow. Value decomposes additively into a bare production block and a correction option specific to the factor 𝜌. The shadow price of reversibility equals the discounted expected volume of corrected errors, a magnitude observable in reversal data — asset sales, liquidation recoveries, exits from activity — which makes the factor empirically identifiable. The value of the option rises with risk in the sense of Rothschild and Stiglitz, and its marginal value rises as the environment deteriorates in the first-order sense, whence a scissors effect — clemency is worth most where agents can least afford it. Optimal reversibility increases with exposure to shocks, and the gap between the optimal and the observed level measures the institutional trap. Since the correction option is convex in 𝜌, half-reforms are dominated whenever the cost of clemency lacks convexity — the optimal regime jumps from one extreme to the other. Finally, reversibility puts a floor under the marginal return of capital, which founds the complementarity between clemency and investment and sheds light on capital flight from irrecoverable environments.

title: Can Responsible AI Exist Without Responsible Institutions? An Institutional Responsibility Framework for AI Governance

detail.title: Can Responsible AI Exist Without Responsible Institutions? An Institutional Responsibility Framework for AI Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competeing interests or personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not requied for this study because it did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, or primary data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any a=funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed governance from a predominantly technical challenge into a normative and institutional one. Although the Responsible AI literature has established widely accepted ethical principles including fairness, accountability, transparency, explainability, and human oversight, it has devoted comparatively little attention to the institutions responsible for translating these principles into legitimate governance. Existing scholarship largely treats institutions as mechanisms for implementing ethical commitments rather than as normative actors whose responsibility itself requires philosophical justification. This article addresses that conceptual gap by asking: Can Responsible AI exist without Responsible Institutions? Using a philosophical and interdisciplinary conceptual analysis, it draws on Responsible AI scholarship, institutional theory, public administration, political philosophy, and digital government to develop Institutional Responsibility as a distinct normative concept and proposes the Institutional Responsibility Framework (IRF) as its principal theoretical contribution. The framework conceptualises responsibility as institutionally constituted, distributed, exercised, justified, and sustained across complex AI governance ecosystems. It argues that Responsible AI presupposes responsible institutions because ethical principles cannot govern AI independently of the institutional arrangements that establish legitimate authority, coordinate governance, and sustain public trust. By relocating responsibility from isolated actors and principle-based compliance to the institutional foundations of governance, the article advances a new philosophical foundation for Responsible AI. It contributes to AI ethics, institutional theory, public administration, and digital government by demonstrating that trustworthy, legitimate, and democratically accountable AI governance ultimately depends upon the existence of responsible institutions rather than ethical principles alone.

title: A Kaldor-Hicks Compensation Scheme for Ride-Hailing Markets With Structural Unemployment Brought by Robotaxis
affiliations: Shenzhen Technology University, Shenzhen Technology University, Shenzhen Technology University and

detail.title: A Kaldor-Hicks Compensation Scheme for Ride-Hailing Markets With Structural Unemployment Brought by Robotaxis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This work is financially supported by grants from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (72201176, 52472326).

detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of robotaxis (RTs) in ride-sourcing markets can improve operational efficiency while simultaneously displacing human drivers and causing potential structural unemployment. This study investigates whether a Kaldor-Hicks (KH) compensation scheme can facilitate an acceptable transition toward RT-integrated ride-sourcing markets. We develop an economic equilibrium model of a monopoly ridesourcing platform operating a mixed fleet of human-driven vehicles and RTs, explicitly incorporating the welfare loss of structurally unemployed drivers. The feasibility of KH compensation is analytically examined under both platform profit maximization and social welfare maximization scenarios. The results show that KH compensation is not always feasible under unconstrained optimization, as its feasibility depends on the RT operating cost and the successful transition rate of displaced drivers. However, when the compensation cost is internalized into the platform's decision-making or social welfare evaluation, KH compensation can always be achieved. Numerical experiments calibrated with data from Shenzhen, China, further validate the analytical findings and demonstrate that accounting for labor market frictions is essential when evaluating the impacts of RT adoption. The study provides policy insights for designing transition mechanisms that balance technological advancement and labor protection in autonomous mobility markets.

title: How Do CCyBs Travel? Internal Capital Markets & Domestic Borrowing
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank, Deutsche Bundesbank, University of Zurich - Department Finance and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: How Do CCyBs Travel? Internal Capital Markets & Domestic Borrowing
detail.abstract: Macroprudential capital buffers are meant to contain risk inside the activating jurisdiction. We show how they travel through multinational firms. Exploiting staggered countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) activations in host countries of German multinationals' foreign subsidiaries, we trace a firm-side leakage channel. Subsidiary bank credit contracts by 10.6 percent per percentage-point CCyB, and falls relative to nonbank credit within the same borrower and quarter; subsidiary total borrowing shows no detectable change across creditor domiciles. German parents replace the lost credit with internal debt and refinance at home, raising the credit-weighted default risk of German lenders' exposure to these groups by about 20 percent of its mean. The affected multinational groups owe German lenders 26 billion euros, the exposure base on which this rerouting operates. With no German CCyB active, risk returns home.

title: White-Collar Crime: An Empirical Examination Of Race, Class, And The Challenges Of Enforcement
affiliations: Chicago-Kent College of Law - Illinois Institute of Technology

detail.title: White-Collar Crime: An Empirical Examination Of Race, Class, And The Challenges Of Enforcement
detail.abstract: The United States loses billions of dollars every year due to white-collar crime, in part because white-collar offenders benefit from underenforcement by authorities. Despite the scale of its economic impact, white-collar crime remains relatively understudied when compared to other forms of criminality. Although recent years have seen increased research attention on white-collar crime, little of this scholarship has considered the effect of offender characteristics on perceptions of culpability and blameworthiness of white-collar offenders. This Article aims to help rectify that shortcoming by using survey experiment methodology to measure perceptions of routine embezzlement versus conventional theft-as well as the effect of offender race and class on those perceptions-to better understand how to improve white-collar crime enforcement. Unlike previous research on perceptions of other kinds of criminality in which race and class have a substantial impact on judgments of culpability, the results of this Article indicate that there are significant differences in judgments of white-collar crime and conventional crime that are not accounted for by offender demographics. Instead, the nature of the criminal activity itself proves most salient. Although respondents deem embezzlement and theft to be equally serious and both worthy of punishment, they are significantly less likely to: (1) define evidence of embezzlement as a crime; (2) express a desire for criminal punishment for white-collar offenders; and (3) report white-collar suspects to police. These results, in conjunction with existing underenforcement of white-collar criminal law, suggest that policymakers should consider alternative forms of civil enforcement to enhance enforcement in the white-collar space. To that end, this Article concludes by outlining two low-cost policy proposals designed to strengthen white-collar civil enforcement in the United States.

title: Critical Infrastructure Concentration and Systemic Financial Fragility: General Model and Proofs Technical Companion Note

detail.title: Critical Infrastructure Concentration and Systemic Financial Fragility: General Model and Proofs Technical Companion Note
detail.abstract: This note is the technical companion to Harker (2026), "Critical Infrastructure Concentration and Systemic Financial Fragility." The main paper develops the analysis in a parametric model in which every result is available in closed form and every proof is a short computation. This companion preserves the analysis at full generality: the general model with arbitrary convex joint-failure loss functions, arbitrary provider cost functions with scale economies, and arbitrary common-cause failure-class structures; the complete set of assumptions; and full proofs, including the fixed-point existence and uniqueness apparatus, the Schur-convexity lemma that connects concentration to system fragility, and the general robust-portfolio characterization. The note contains only the technical material; the running example, literature review, calibration, and policy discussion are in the main paper. Each document is self-contained; results are numbered independently. Readers interested in the policy argument should read the main paper; readers interested in the mathematics at full generality should read this note alongside it.

title: Brief for Amicus Curiae, Professor John Yun in Support of Appellant, X Corp. v. World Federation of Advertisers (5th Cir. No. 26-10394)
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: Brief for Amicus Curiae, Professor John Yun in Support of Appellant, X Corp. v. World Federation of Advertisers (5th Cir. No. 26-10394)
detail.abstract: This amicus brief critiques the district court's holding that a group boycott plaintiff suffers antitrust injury only when the challenged coordination involves the plaintiff's competitor(s). Specifically, when members of a trade association jointly negotiate to improve the bargaining terms on which they deal with a trading partner, the harm falls directly on that partner, as in Professional Engineers, Trial Lawyers, and Indiana Federation of Dentists. Fifth Circuit precedent likewise confirms that a horizontal agreement need not involve, directly or indirectly, the victim's competitors; thus, the district court improperly narrowed the standing requirement. Additionally, an anticompetitive agreement may be manifested through an authority delegated to trade association leadership—such as, in the Supreme Court’s decision in Hydrolevel—so that Twombly's conscious-parallelism concerns are not implicated.

title: Has The Dragon Been Tamed? Making Sense Of One Hundred And Fifty Years Of "History And Traditions" In A Post- Dobbs, Bruen, And Kennedy World
affiliations: Michigan State University - Michigan State Law Review

detail.title: Has The Dragon Been Tamed? Making Sense Of One Hundred And Fifty Years Of "History And Traditions" In A Post- Dobbs, Bruen, And Kennedy World
detail.abstract:
Justice Holmes wrote that history is like a dragon; once you have counted all the teeth and scales, you either slay it to overcome it or you tame it to make it useful. Recently, the Supreme Court has released a trilogy of opinions, Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, New York Pistol & Rifle Ass'n, Inc. v. Bruen, and Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, which all implement a new "history and tradition test." This history and tradition approach has vast implications for lower courts addressing the issues implicated in these cases, regardless of whether it is a federal court or state high court. But where did this shift towards history and tradition constitutional interpretation come from? More importantly, how has this shift impacted the decisions of lower courts?
The history and tradition test was not made from whole cloth as this kind of constitutional interpretation has its own historical record and traditional implementation through the Court's earliest due process cases. Once the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified, history and tradition became one of the cornerstones for the incorporation doctrine. Additionally, history and tradition would be used to identify new rights, such as a right to abortion under Roe v. Wade.
Throughout the twentieth century, history and tradition evidence served as a useful guidepost to demarcate the outer bounds of constitutional interpretation. But then, the Court issued Dobbs, Bruen, and Kennedy; each of these cases introduced history and tradition analysis as the preferable means to address constitutional claims involving abortion, firearms, and religious prayer performed by state employees. To make sense of this monumental shift, this Note delves into the opinions issued by lower courts that have had to grapple with the idiosyncrasies of the Court’s newly minted the test for constitutional interpretation. This Note attempts to make suggestions on how these sources of information can be better utilized

reference: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Working Paper Forthcoming
title: Is the AI Boom Volatility-Biased Technological Change?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City and Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City

detail.title: Is the AI Boom Volatility-Biased Technological Change?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Working Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We show that AI technologies are oriented toward jobs and workers that typically exhibit greater volatility in labor market outcomes over the business cycle. Occupations currently most exposed to AI are those that have historically exhibited (i) greater volatility in employment levels over business cycles, (ii) higher job-switching rates by workers, (iii) higher job-finding rates, and (iv) a lower likelihood for workers to exit the labor force following a job loss. The sectors of the U.S. economy that produce AI technologies have also historically exhibited high volatility in productivity. We then quantify how technology-led structural changes in economic activities contribute to aggregate business cycle volatility. Growth in the production of AI-based technologies in recent years increased the volatility of U.S. output by 2.8 percent, roughly 3.5 times what resulted from the late 1990s' IT boom. If the orientation of AI toward occupations that exhibit higher variability in labor market outcomes results in a higher aggregate labor supply elasticity, the effects on aggregate volatility are even greater.

title: From Point Thresholds to Probability Distributions in AI Radiology: A Monte Carlo Break-even Analysis of AI-assisted Radiology

detail.title: From Point Thresholds to Probability Distributions in AI Radiology: A Monte Carlo Break-even Analysis of AI-assisted Radiology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests. The author has no financial relationship with, and has received no compensation or in-kind support from, any developer, vendor, or purchaser of artificial intelligence software for radiology.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Deterministic decision-analytic models of artificial intelligence deployment in radiology identify disease-prevalence thresholds at which AI-assisted interpretation and human-only interpretation have equal expected cost. These thresholds depend on implementation architecture. Sequential AI triage may be economically favorable below a threshold because AI-negative studies can avoid human interpretation. Under concurrent AI-radiologist reading, the economic relationship instead depends on the adjudication rule. Disjunctive, or OR, adjudication increases sensitivity while reducing specificity and can become economically favorable at higher prevalence. Conjunctive, or AND, adjudication increases specificity while reducing sensitivity and can instead be economically favorable at lower prevalence. Human-final-arbiter adjudication has no interpretation-cost break-even under the maintained assumptions.

 These results are conventionally expressed as point thresholds derived from fixed values of diagnostic performance and economic inputs. In practice, AI sensitivity, AI specificity, human performance, software cost, and the downstream costs of false-positive and false-negative decisions are uncertain. The break-even prevalence should therefore itself be treated as an uncertain quantity rather than as a perfectly known boundary.

 This study develops a Monte Carlo extension of the existing break-even framework. Uncertainty in operating characteristics and cost parameters is propagated through the previously derived OR and AND threshold functions to generate distributions of break-even prevalence. The analysis also estimates the probability that a feasible threshold exists and the probability that each concurrent-reading strategy is economically favorable at a specified disease prevalence. Human-final-arbiter adjudication is retained as a structural no-break-even case.

 The simulations show that parameter uncertainty does not systematically favor or disfavor AI-assisted interpretation and does not overturn the underlying direction of the deterministic relationships. Instead, it transforms a single break-even point into a distribution of possible thresholds and converts a binary economic conclusion into a prevalence-dependent probability transition. For OR adjudication, the probability that AI-assisted reading is economically favorable rises as disease prevalence increases. For AND adjudication, that probability falls as prevalence increases, and uncertainty also affects whether a feasible break-even exists at all. The practical implication is that procurement and health technology assessment should consider not only a deterministic break-even prevalence, but also the probability that a proposed AI deployment is economically favorable at the disease prevalence relevant to the institution.

title: Institutional Readiness for Responsible AI in the Public Sector: A Theory-informed Framework for AI Governance in Developing Countries

detail.title: Institutional Readiness for Responsible AI in the Public Sector: A Theory-informed Framework for AI Governance in Developing Countries

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because the study involved analysis of publicly available policy, strategy, and regulatory documents and did not involve human participants or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming public sector governance by enhancing decision making, service delivery, and administrative efficiency. However, its rapid adoption has intensified concerns about fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, and democratic legitimacy. Although Responsible AI scholarship has advanced ethical principles, governance frameworks, and implementation strategies, insufficient attention has been paid to the institutional conditions required for responsible AI governance. This article addresses this gap by introducing institutional readiness as a distinct analytical construct and developing the Institutional Readiness Framework (IRF): A Theory-Informed Framework for Responsible AI Governance. Drawing on institutional theory, public administration, and Responsible AI scholarship, this conceptual study synthesizes existing literature to identify the governance capabilities required for effective AI governance in the public sector. The IRF conceptualizes institutional readiness through seven interrelated dimensions: leadership and strategic vision; regulatory and policy capacity; organizational capacity; technical and digital capability; accountability and ethical oversight; stakeholder collaboration and public engagement; and institutional learning and adaptive capacity. The article contributes by introducing institutional readiness as a missing dimension in Responsible AI scholarship, integrating three complementary theoretical traditions into a coherent governance framework, and providing a foundation for future empirical research and policy development, particularly in developing-country contexts. It argues that responsible AI depends fundamentally on institutions with the capability to govern AI ethically, effectively, and sustainably.

title: The Two-job Professional: Moonlighting, Overemployment, and the Unraveling Loyalty Contract in India's Knowledge Economy

detail.title: The Two-job Professional: Moonlighting, Overemployment, and the Unraveling Loyalty Contract in India's Knowledge Economy

declarations.ethicsApproval: This is a conceptual and argumentative working paper. It does not report the results of an empirical study involving patients, human participants, personal data, surveys, interviews, focus groups, experiments, or animal subjects. All evidence used in the paper is drawn from publicly available sources—including published news reporting, regulatory and court documents, industry reports, company disclosures, and openly accessible online commentary—and is cited accordingly. No primary data were collected from identifiable individuals, and no confidential or personal information was obtained or analysed. Consequently, no review or approval from an institutional ethics committee, institutional review board (IRB), or equivalent body was required for this work. No case-study consent was necessary, as the paper does not present individual case studies of identifiable persons. The author has no competing interests or funding sources to declare in relation to this paper.

detail.abstract: A quiet but significant shift is underway in India's knowledge workforce. A growing number of software engineers, product managers, data analysts, and mid-level consultants are simultaneously holding two, and occasionally more, paid roles-sometimes openly, often invisibly. What was once called "moonlighting" and treated as a disciplinary offense has, under the combined pressure of remote work, wage compression, gig platforms, and generative-AI tooling, mutated into something more structural: deliberate overemployment. This paper argues that the dominant corporate response-exclusivity clauses, moonlighting bans, attendance surveillance, and occasional public terminations-has become a form of compliance theater. It neither prevents dual employment nor addresses the reasons professionals seek it. Drawing on the Indian information technology and business-process management context, with comparisons to the wider overemployment movement, the paper traces the collapse of the mid-twentiethcentury loyalty bargain, in which long tenure was exchanged for predictable progression and retirement security. That bargain has been hollowed out by bench policies, variable pay, layoff cycles, and the erosion of defined-benefit security. The paper offers practitioners a four-principle framework-outcomes over presence, disclosure over prohibition, reciprocity in writing, and honesty about career shape-for renegotiating the employment compact. For leaders who need to retain committed attention in the 2020s, the choice is no longer whether to accommodate this reality, but how.

title: Criminal Background Checks: Implications For Discrimination And Crime
affiliations: Texas A&M University (TAMU), Central Texas

detail.title: Criminal Background Checks: Implications For Discrimination And Crime
detail.abstract:
Criminal background checks have recently attracted the attention of scholars and policymakers. Reformers argue that such checks present an unreasonable burden on marginalized individuals and brand them with a stigma they do not deserve. Proponents insist that such checks are necessary to protect the safety of communities and allow other individuals to make informed decisions about their own safety. Yet one profound aspect of the issue has gone surprisingly unnoticed by reformers and proponents alike: the quality of background checks. To what extent do these checks indeed provide accurate information about individuals? 

This Article offers a deep dive into the history, evolution, and contemporary practice of "rap sheets," which are documents containing information on arrests and prosecution, used as inputs for common criminal background checks. It finds that the Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) fingerprint-assisted Triple-I database frequently used by landlords, employers, and neighbors-is deeply flawed. It is missing critical information, reports arrests even if the individual is later acquitted, misidentifies plea bargain information, and fails to account for jurisdictional differences. The sobering conclusion about the failure of this system also suggests practical solutions. 

Drawing on successful models of consumer reporting agencies (CRAs), this Article offers a blueprint for reform. While reform cannot resolve all debates around background checks, it can alleviate unfair stigmatization, improve the reintegration of criminal suspects, enhance deterrence goals, and better protect communities.

title: The Cultural Department Paradox: A Logical Derivation of the Multiplicative Nature of Organizational Culture Functions
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Cultural Department Paradox: A Logical Derivation of the Multiplicative Nature of Organizational Culture Functions
detail.abstract: Almost every large organization maintains a dedicated cultural department-a unit responsible for internal events, team-building activities, value promotion, and employee engagement. Yet the fundamental nature of this department within the firm's production function remains insufficiently examined. This paper asks a foundational question: Is the cultural department a base value that directly generates output, or a multiplier that amplifies existing productive capacity? Employing a three-hypothesis exhaustive elimination method-the cultural department is either (1) a base value, (2) a null effect, or (3) a multiplicative multiplier-this paper demonstrates through logical derivation that only the multiplier hypothesis holds. This conclusion is corroborated by two empirical observations: large firms universally maintain cultural departments while small firms do not, suggesting a scale threshold; and during economic downturns, cultural department budgets are the first to be cut, indicating they are treated as discretionary multipliers rather than essential base functions. The paper further suggests that this logical framework can be extended to other organizational functions-such as legal, compliance, and human resources-offering a generalizable analytical lens for distinguishing base departments from multiplier departments in organizational design.

reference: William & Mary Law School Research Paper Forthcoming; Harvard Environmental Law Review (forthcoming)
title: Unsustainable Presidential Administration
affiliations: William & Mary Law School

detail.title: Unsustainable Presidential Administration

publicationDetails.detailsText: William & Mary Law School Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: William & Mary Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The first Trump Administration prioritized speed and salience over legal soundness, and its unilateral deregulatory efforts—some fairly characterized as "regulatory slop"—were largely undone once Trump left office. This essay argues that the second Trump Administration, despite being more prepared and more aggressive, has not learned this lesson: it continues to elevate executive branch unilateralism over the slower, harder work of legislative or judicial engagement. The administration’s reliance upon executive orders and unilateral action has sacrificed sustainability for speed. Where the administration’s efforts are most likely to result in lasting legal or policy change, the administration is relying upon cooperation with other branches, such as by working with Congress to pass Congressional Review Act resolutions or prompting judicial review and endorsement of new understandings of existing environmental laws.The Administration's unilateral actions may be consequential, but they are not sustainable: lasting change to environmental law will come only through legislation or judicial ratification, not executive decree alone.

title: Originalism As Anti-Woman: An Examination Of Dobbs And Bruen
affiliations: Mercer University School of Law

detail.title: Originalism As Anti-Woman: An Examination Of Dobbs And Bruen
detail.abstract:
In recent years, the United States Supreme Court's problematic commitment to originalism has strengthened. An originalist mode of constitutional interpretation is particularly concerning for women, who were excluded from the democratic and lawmaking process at the time the Constitution was enacted and who were considered legally inferior to men. 

The deeply anti-woman issues with originalism are exemplified in two recent blockbuster opinions: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, in which the Court not only overturned Roe v. Wade, but also determined the Constitution does not protect the right to obtain an abortion; and New York State Rifle and Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen, in which the Court held the Second Amendment right to bear arms extends to public carry of a handgun. Each of these cases begins with an anti-women "input" by requiring courts to adopt the worldview of people who did not believe that women were entitled to the same legal rights as men. Each case results in an anti-woman "output" because the policy results of this interpretive frame harm women. 

This Article examines how, in Dobbs and Bruen, the Court relied problematically on an anti-woman originalist mode of constitutional interpretation. It then reviews some of the devastating outcomes that have harmed women in their aftermath. This Article concludes by proposing bold solutions for constitutional interpretation moving forward by addressing both the importance of expressive messaging coming from the Court and the creation of a form of legal analysis that works to support women.

title: The Divided Subject and the Symbolic Garment Psychoanalysis, Sexuation, and the Fashioning of Modern Femininity
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Divided Subject and the Symbolic Garment Psychoanalysis, Sexuation, and the Fashioning of Modern Femininity
detail.abstract: This monograph develops a theoretical framework for understanding modern femininity not as a fixed essence but as a set of historically variable technologies for managing an ineliminable psychic impossibility: the non-coincidence of the subject with the image through which she seeks recognition. Rather than treating psychoanalysis as a repository of static claims about "woman," the argument traces feminine subjectivity from Freud's early and unfinished speculations, through the object-relational and culturalist revisions of Klein, Horney, and Deutsch, to Lacan's formalization of the divided subject, the phallic signifier, the objet petit a, the gaze, jouissance, and the formulas of sexuation. This apparatus is then set to work alongside Beauvoir's existentialist account of woman as situation, Irigaray's and Butler's deconstructions of sexual difference, Mulvey's theory of the cinematic gaze, Barthes's and Baudrillard's semiotics of the fashion-sign, Bourdieu's sociology of taste and distinction, and Foucault's account of disciplinary and confessional technologies of the self. The synthesis that results proposes that haute couture, perfume advertising, cinema, feminist critique, psychoanalytic treatment, and contemporary self-branding are not successive replacements of one another but structurally related attempts to give a barred subject a stable symbolic form. Chanel and Saint Laurent are treated not as objects "explained" by theory but as historical sites where this structural impossibility becomes visible, marketable, and endlessly repeatable. The monograph closes by considering the ethical stakes of an image that promises closure it cannot deliver, and by asking what forms of feminine subjectivity become thinkable once that promise is understood as structural rather than personal.

title: Leadership Characteristic and Loyalty
affiliations: , Politeknik Tuanku Sultanah Bahiyah and Seberang Perai Polytechnic, Penang, Malaysia

detail.title: Leadership Characteristic and Loyalty
detail.abstract: Performance is a priority for the organization to keep remaining in the market. Leadership characteristics are required to build up and increase loyalty among the employees. Throughout, good characteristics, for instance listening skills, empathy, and ability to motivate, may cause employees to be happy and satisfaction to lead loyalty. In addition, loyalty can contribute to better employee performance where they utilize skills, experience, and knowledge to achieve objectives. This study discusses how good leadership characteristics can enhance loyalty and vice versa. Performance is also related to leadership characteristics, where an employee is willing to work for the organization if they have a good relationship with the leader.

title: The Organisation as the Executable Unit: Towards an Executable Organisational Operating Model for AI-Native Software Engineering
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Organisation as the Executable Unit: Towards an Executable Organisational Operating Model for AI-Native Software Engineering
detail.abstract: Software engineering has historically depended on organisational structures, shared objectives, delegated authority, reviewed decisions, and institutional knowledge that outlives any individual contributor, to sustain systems across changes in personnel and technology. Contemporary artificial intelligence systems increasingly perform substantial engineering work, including code generation, architectural proposal, and review, yet operate largely outside these organisational structures: without delegated authority, without persistent organisational responsibility, and without accountability that survives the interaction in which a decision was made. The paper argues that this absence of organisational structure, not insufficient model capability, is the primary obstacle to safely extending AI autonomy across the software engineering lifecycle. It proposes an executable organisational operating model in which the organisation itself is the unit that persists, not the individual participant or the AI agent. Objectives justify capabilities. Capabilities expose governed services. Services are delivered through accountable roles. Roles are fulfilled by interchangeable participants. Those participants may be human, artificial, or external. They produce artefacts, evidence, and organisational knowledge. The paper distinguishes this approach from existing agent-orchestration and workflow-coordination systems, which coordinate interactions and activities but do not execute an organisation with explicit authority, accountability, and institutional memory. It discusses the conditions under which this becomes necessary as the number of autonomous participants in an engineering organisation grows, the limitations of governance as a guarantee of process rather than judgement, and the extension of the model beyond software engineering to other knowledge-intensive domains.

title: The Yin and Yang of Organizational Silence: The Mediating Role of Psychological Safety and Attachment Orientations in Organizational Commitment and Burnout
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Yin and Yang of Organizational Silence: The Mediating Role of Psychological Safety and Attachment Orientations in Organizational Commitment and Burnout

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest, personal relationships, or financial competing interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this manuscript, as it is a purely conceptual/theoretical study that did not involve human participants, animal subjects, patients, or empirical data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or non-profit sectors. The study was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Why do employees often choose not to speak up, even when they have something meaningful to say? This paper argues that part of the answer lies in early relational history. Drawing on Adult Attachment Theory and Social Exchange Theory, it proposes a conceptual framework linking individual attachment orientations (secure, anxious, avoidant, and disorganized) to workplace silence through the mediating mechanism of psychological safety (Hazan & Shaver, 1990; Edmondson, 1999). Rather than treating silence as a single, uniform behavior, the framework distinguishes its destructive forms, defensive and acquiescent silence ("Yin"), from its constructive form, prosocial silence ("Yang") (Van Dyne, Ang, & Botero, 2003). The model further traces how each pathway shapes emotional burnout and affective organizational commitment, drawing on recent meta-analytic evidence that links attachment insecurity to burnout (Warnock, Ju, & Katz, 2024) and links psychological safety to silence behavior (Hao et al., 2022; Sherf, Parke, & Isaakyan, 2021). The paper closes with practical recommendations for HR and leadership practice, and it outlines a specific empirical gap this framework is positioned to address. Namely, whether secure attachment predicts greater engagement in prosocial silence specifically, rather than merely less negative silence.

title: Audi Sport (Volkswagen Group) Leading in the Luxury High-performance Market while Embracing Electrification

detail.title: Audi Sport (Volkswagen Group) Leading in the Luxury High-performance Market while Embracing Electrification
detail.abstract: Audi Sport faces critical strategic challenges as it navigates the transformation of the premium automotive segment towards electrification and sustainability. This analysis evaluates the division's capabilities and opportunities within the Volkswagen Group's Progressive brand portfolio, focusing on maintaining premium performance positioning while embracing technological innovation. The external environment shows increasing complexity in competitive dynamics, with both traditional manufacturers and new technology companies competing for market share. Key challenges include battery technology limitations, charging infrastructure standardization, manufacturing sustainability, and diverse regional market requirements. Internally, Audi Sport builds on its strong engineering expertise and motorsport heritage while developing new capabilities in electric vehicle technology and digital integration. The division is actively pursuing technological transformation through specialized electric platforms and the Volkswagen Group's Cariad software initiative. Substantial electric vehicle production and sales growth demonstrate strong commitment to this transition. Success in this transformation requires balancing traditional performance values with new sustainability demands through strategic initiatives in electric powertrain innovation, digital platform integration, market specific electrification strategies, and motorsport excellence. The implementation roadmap outlines a phased approach from establishing digital infrastructure to developing autonomous ecosystem capabilities. Strategic resource allocation across financial, human capital, and technological domains, supported by comprehensive risk management and performance monitoring systems, will be crucial for success. Through systematic execution of these strategies, Audi Sport can maintain its leadership position while driving the redefinition of premium performance in an electrified automotive future. By focusing on these core areas, Audi Sport is positioned to leverage its heritage and capabilities to lead the premium performance segment's transition to sustainable mobility, ensuring long-term competitive advantage in an evolving market landscape

title: Adapting Auto Specs Grading for the AI Era: An in-class Approach

detail.title: Adapting Auto Specs Grading for the AI Era: An in-class Approach

Sources were verified and compiled by the authors. All human subjects provided informed consent and the study was approved by St. Mary’s College of Maryland Institutional Review Board. All data is sensitive and cannot be provided.
